items.title: Péage et pesage : trois sites pressentis à Port-Gentil
items.description: Trois sites pressentis pour les futures stations de péage et de pesage : le ministre des Travaux publics, Edgard Moukoumbi, s’est rendu à Port-Gentil, dans l’Ogooué-Maritime, le 9 octobre, pour les repérer sur le terrain. Cette mission, conduite au titre des orientations gouvernementales, concerne un projet validé en Conseil des ministres le 18 septembre. L’objectif est de « renforcer la sécurité routière » et de préserver le patrimoine routier national. Le ministre des Travaux publics, Edgard Moukoumbi, et sa délégation sur le terrain, à Port-Gentil. © D.R. Trois sites potentiels ont été retenus pour accueillir ces futures stations : en amont du pont Ozouri (dans le sens Port-Gentil-Omboué), à Onguedjo et au carrefour Omboué. Cette étape doit toutefois être complétée par des études techniques approfondies, en vue de préciser les caractéristiques des sites et de préparer la mise en œuvre du projet. En marge de cette reconnaissance, le chef du département en charge des Travaux publics a échangé avec les entreprises chargées des futurs travaux d’aménagement des voiries et des ouvrages hydrauliques de Port-Gentil. Il a insisté sur l’accélération des préparatifs techniques, préalable au lancement effectif des chantiers. « J’ai insisté sur la nécessité d’accélérer la réalisation des études d’exécution afin de permettre leur validation dans les meilleurs délais et d’engager les procédures nécessaires au suivi et au contrôle des travaux », a-t-il souligné, appelant ainsi à davantage de célérité dans la conduite des projets. Cette démarche s’inscrit dans l’anticipation des besoins en infrastructures de la capitale économique, notamment à l’approche de la 5ᵉ édition de la fête de la Libération, prévue en 2028 dans l’Ogooué-Maritime. Pour Edgard Moukoumbi, l’enjeu est de transformer les orientations gouvernementales en réalisations, au bénéfice des usagers. « Nous devons anticiper et accélérer la réalisation des projets structurants pour offrir à nos populations des infrastructures modernes, durables et adaptées à leurs besoins », a-t-il plaidé. items.title: Joseph Cudjoe writes: Ghana must break free from the dangerous mindset that natural resources are the foundation for wealth
items.description: “Resources are not; they become.” This famous observation by economist Erich W. Zimmermann should challenge one of the most deeply rooted misconceptions in Ghana’s development thinking: the belief that our natural resource endowment is the foundation of our prosperity. We have become so obsessed with what lies beneath our soil that we risk underestimating what lies within our people. We celebrate gold, bauxite, manganese and lithium, yet pay insufficient attention to the knowledge, skills, innovation and productive capabilities that transform nations into economic powerhouses. Countries such as Singapore, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, Denmark, the Netherlands and Luxembourg have demonstrated that abundant natural resource wealth is not a prerequisite for national prosperity. Their experiences show what education, skills, innovation, technology and industrial development can achieve. We must stop conditioning Ghana’s youth to believe that our natural resources are the foundation of our wealth. Our greatest resource must be our people and their ability to think, innovate, invent, manufacture and solve problems. Ghana should invest heavily in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) education to equip young people with the capabilities to create technologies, develop products and build competitive industries. Mineral deposits can be depleted or lose their market value, but human ingenuity can continually create new industries, products and sources of wealth. Ghana must invest in its people as seriously as it exploits its minerals. History reinforces this thinking. Aluminium was once more expensive than gold until technological advances made it affordable. Natural ultramarine, once more expensive than gold by weight, lost much of its commercial importance when synthetic alternatives emerged. Natural alum, once vital to textile dyeing, was displaced by manufactured chemicals. Flint lost its importance with the development of metalworking, while asbestos declined sharply after its deadly health effects became known. Even natural saltpetre and guano lost much of their strategic value as industrial alternatives emerged. These resources once generated substantial wealth for the nations that controlled them. If materials once considered indispensable can lose their value, why should Ghana build its economic future around the assumption that our minerals will always command the same importance they do today? Our gold, bauxite, manganese and lithium present opportunities, but opportunities are not guarantees of lasting prosperity. Technological breakthroughs, alternative materials, recycling and changing industrial needs can alter demand and prices. Ghana must therefore move beyond the obsession with extracting and exporting natural resources. We must invest in education, technical skills, scientific research, technology, manufacturing and enterprise. Where economically viable, we should process our minerals locally and use the proceeds to develop industries that can survive beyond mineral booms. The fundamental question is not how much wealth nature has deposited beneath our feet, but how much productive capacity we have developed above the ground. OUR FUTURE MUST BE EXTRACTED FROM OUR PEOPLE, NOT FROM THE GROUND. Human resources, when continuously developed, can renew and expand their value, while natural resources are finite and can be depleted. Human capabilities can also adapt to emerging global needs through education, innovation and skills development in ways that mineral deposits cannot. Ghana therefore cannot continue to teach its young people, implicitly or explicitly, that our natural resource endowment is the principal answer to our economic challenges. Such a mindset risks producing a nation that is rich in minerals but poor in innovation, employment creation and industrial capability. Natural resources provide potential; human knowledge, productivity and innovation turn that potential into lasting wealth. Our national ambition must be to raise generations of highly skilled and innovative Ghanaians capable of creating products, developing technologies, building competitive businesses and exporting knowledge to the world. The countries that will prosper tomorrow will not necessarily be those with the richest mineral deposits, but those with the most capable people and the strongest capacity to innovate. Ghana must prepare its youth to create wealth, not merely to inherit the hope that wealth lies beneath our soil. MY QUESTION The Akufo-Addo and Bawumia administration demonstrated this understanding through its education policies. Is the Mahama administration investing enough in STEM education, and doing more, to equip our youth with the knowledge, skills and technological capabilities to create wealth beyond our natural resources?

items.title: Produits laitiers, conserves, cosmétiques, insecticides : 250 kg de marchandises incinérés à Lambaréné
items.description: Près de 250 kg de produits impropres à la consommation sont partis en fumée : le 9 octobre 2026, l’Agence gabonaise de sécurité alimentaire (AGASA) a procédé à leur incinération à Lambaréné, pour protéger les consommateurs et renforcer la sécurité sanitaire des aliments. Ces produits avaient été saisis lors de contrôles effectués dans plusieurs commerces du Moyen-Ogooué. Les produits en incinération. © AGP Sur le site de la décharge publique de Nzelabola, au PK 5 sur la route nationale 1 (RN1), la délégation provinciale de l’AGASA a incinéré les marchandises non conformes, en collaboration avec le parquet près le tribunal de première instance de Lambaréné. Conduite par le délégué provincial de l’AGASA, Brice Maloula, cette intervention s’est tenue en présence du substitut du procureur de la République, Orchie Flora Owele, mandatée par le parquet, ainsi que des agents de l’Agence. Les produits détruits avaient été saisis en septembre lors d’inspections menées dans plusieurs commerces de Lambaréné, Makouké et Bifoun. Le lot incinéré comprenait notamment 117,18 kg de produits laitiers, 10,2 kg de conserves, 5 kg de produits frais, 1,29 kg de denrées alimentaires diverses, 56,25 litres de boissons non alcoolisées, 27,48 kg de produits cosmétiques et 25,10 kg de produits divers. Du poisson non identifié, du piment et des insecticides figuraient également parmi les marchandises saisies. Des contrôles réguliers pour prévenir les risques sanitaires Pour le parquet, cette opération s’inscrit dans le cadre de la protection de la santé publique et de la lutte contre la commercialisation de produits dangereux pour les consommateurs. Orchie Flora Owele a rappelé que les auteurs d’infractions liées à la mise sur le marché de denrées impropres à la consommation s’exposent à des poursuites judiciaires. De son côté, Brice Maloula a souligné que l’AGASA mène chaque trimestre des campagnes d’inspection visant à vérifier les conditions de conservation et de manipulation des denrées alimentaires, ainsi que le respect des règles d’hygiène et de qualité. Au-delà de la destruction des marchandises saisies, ces opérations visent également à sensibiliser les commerçants et les opérateurs économiques à leurs obligations. Par ces contrôles réguliers, l’AGASA entend renforcer la surveillance du marché local et limiter les risques sanitaires liés à la commercialisation de produits avariés ou non conformes aux normes en vigueur. items.title: Djibouti : le naufrage d’une embarcation de migrants fait au moins 109 morts et 116 portés disparus
Children among 109 dead after boat capsizes off Djibouti, UN says
items.description: At least 109 migrants, including 15 children, have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) has said. The boat was travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 350 people on board when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 80 people were rescued, the IOM said. IOM’s Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a “stark reminder” of the dangers migrants face while seeking a new life elsewhere. Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, according to the UN agency. In a statement on Friday, the organisation said 52 men, 42 women, nine girls and six boys were among the bodies recovered. “This is a devastating loss of life,” Coissac said. “Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives,” he added. Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors – all Ethiopian nationals – have medical care readily available to them. Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war which has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict – and growing instability across the wider region – migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change. Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix has observed more than 20,000 “movements” from Ethiopia to Djibouti. IOM said it is providing assistance to 64 of the survivors at its response centre in Obock, including healthcare and support to “restore contact with their families”. The UN agency is working in “close collaboration” with local authorities to help migrants and “prevent deaths at sea and on land”, it added. According to IOM figures, more than 900 migrants died or went missing taking the same route in 2025, with an 18% increase in the number of people attempting the journey. In March 2026, nine people were killed, and 45 were missing after a similar incident.

items.title: «Vaincre ou mourir» : le livre-boussole de Yannick Flores Moussavou
items.description: « La vie ne récompense pas ceux qui espèrent. Elle couronne ceux qui osent ! » Cette conviction, Yannick Flores Moussavou veut la porter auprès de la jeunesse gabonaise, avec une ambition : promouvoir le leadership, la confiance en soi et la résilience. Son ouvrage « Vaincre ou mourir : le secret d’une vie qui compte pour impacter » a été présenté le 10 octobre 2026 à Libreville, lors d’une cérémonie de vernissage et de dédicace. Photo de famille à l'issue de la présentation, le 10 octobre 2026 à Libreville. © GabonReview Composé de 145 pages réparties en 15 chapitres, « Vaincre ou mourir » est un livre de développement personnel, de leadership et de motivation, qui se veut une boussole pour les jeunes désireux de relever les défis de leur époque. Préfacé par la Dre Marie Lucie Ngayambena et M. Papa Alioune Ndoye, l’ouvrage défend un message central : « La vie ne récompense pas ceux qui espèrent. Elle couronne ceux qui osent ! » À travers cette publication, l’auteur ambitionne de contribuer à l’émergence d’une jeunesse gabonaise capable de participer activement à la construction du Gabon de la Ve République. L’auteur face à son public, une vue du livre et un moment de la cérémonie. © GabonReview Pour l’auteur gabonais Yannick Flores Moussavou, le choix du titre « Vaincre ou mourir » traduit avant tout un appel à la résistance face aux épreuves, aux pressions sociales et aux désillusions. L’auteur invite les jeunes à lutter contre leurs faiblesses, à se méfier des fausses amitiés et à dépasser les apparences, notamment celles véhiculées sur les réseaux sociaux. « Il est important de résister, résister contre les faiblesses, résister contre les oppressions, contre les fausses compagnies, les fausses amitiés, résister contre les désillusions », a-t-il expliqué. Pour lui, cette capacité à résister est indispensable pour s’affirmer et trouver sa place dans la société. Dans sa préface, la Dre Marie Lucie Ngayambena souligne l’engagement de ce jeune auteur en faveur de la formation d’une élite jeune, instruite et déterminée à tracer son chemin. Elle présente l’ouvrage comme une réponse à des enjeux majeurs de notre époque, notamment la lutte pour la survie et la nécessité de se positionner dans une société exigeante. Cette lecture rejoint la vision panafricaine de l’auteur, qui souhaite voir la jeunesse africaine, et gabonaise en particulier, devenir un catalyseur d’excellence et d’exemplarité. La portée de l’ouvrage saluée par la municipalité Présent à la cérémonie, le maire du 2e arrondissement de Libreville, Richard Obiang Ava, a salué la portée de l’ouvrage, qu’il considère comme un plaidoyer pour la jeunesse gabonaise. Il a notamment relevé plusieurs thématiques abordées dans le livre, parmi lesquelles la santé mentale, le leadership féminin et la confiance en soi. La rencontre a également enregistré la participation de plusieurs personnalités, dont la responsable associative gabonaise Haresse Kengue. Au-delà de la présentation d’une œuvre littéraire, cette cérémonie a mis en lumière la volonté de l’auteur de faire de l’écriture un outil de sensibilisation et de transformation sociale. En encourageant les jeunes à oser, à persévérer et à prendre leur destin en main, Yannick Flores Moussavou entend contribuer à l’émergence d’une génération consciente de ses responsabilités et engagée dans le développement du Gabon. items.title: OmniBSIC Bank’s 11th health walk promotes fitness and business growth
items.description: OmniBSIC Bank has held its 11th annual Health Walk at the University of Ghana Sports Stadium, bringing together staff, customers, businesses and members of the public to promote physical fitness, healthy living and networking. The 12-kilometre walk took participants through major routes around Legon City Mall, PRESEC Legon, Atomic Junction, Madina Zongo Junction and Ritz Junction before returning to the stadium. Chairperson of the Health Walk Committee, Akyaa Afreh Arhin Addo-Kufuor, said the event has become a fixture on the bank’s annual calendar, with participants returning each year because of the quality of activities and the attention given to their safety and comfort. She said the bank has maintained the consistency of the initiative by ensuring that each edition meets participants’ expectations. “We don’t just get up and walk. We have experienced instructors, aerobics instructors. We have experienced brass band people who would give us music on the way,” she said. She added that the bank also prioritises security to ensure participants feel safe throughout the activity. “We work as hard as we worked for the first edition,” she said, stressing the bank’s commitment to maintaining the event’s standards as participation grows. Head of the Corporate Communications Department, Justin Carl Arhin, said the turnout, energy and networking among participants demonstrated the value of the initiative beyond promoting physical fitness. He noted that the event also provides opportunities for exhibitors and businesses to connect with potential customers and generate economic activity. “Look around you, see the numbers, see the energy, see the vibe, see the networking that is going on, see the number of exhibitors who have been able to come and the kind of economic transformation that we are also achieving as a result of all the business that is going on here,” he said. Mr Arhin said the bank was pleased with the outcome and intended to sustain the initiative, adding that it would continue to grow in scale and participation. OmniBSIC Bank says it remains committed to initiatives that promote healthy living, strengthen community relationships and create opportunities for businesses to engage with customers beyond the banking hall.

items.title: Una madrugada de huidas y otro campamento desalojado en Ceuta
items.description: A las ocho de la mañana, las luces azules de los furgones policiales avanzan hacia la explanada de El Guano . A poca distancia queda la playa de El Trampolín, donde cientos de migrantes malvivieron durante más de dos meses . Aquella franja de arena también sirvió de plató de televisión y congregó a docenas de periodistas llegados para contar una crisis que cambió el paisaje de Ceuta. Pero el movimiento había empezado de madrugada. Numerosos jóvenes recogieron sus pertenencias y se marcharon antes de que llegara la Policía. Algunos corrieron hacia el monte, sin advertir que un dron policial vigilaba la zona desde el aire. La víspera ya sospechaban que el desalojo estaba cerca. “¿Mañana Marruecos?“, preguntaban. Otros enseñaban documentos que guardaban como un tesoro y con la que pretendían acreditar que eran menores de edad. Habían llegado durante las entradas masivas del 30 y 31 de julio y, después de semanas a la intemperie, todavía desconocían qué iba a ocurrir con ellos. Seguir leyendo

items.title: MMA : Abdoulaye Kane terrasse Badr Medkouri et relance sa dynamique
items.description: Abdoulaye Kane a signé une victoire retentissante face au Marocain Badr Medkouri, samedi 10 octobre, à Casablanca. Engagé dans le combat principal de l’événement PFL Africa, le poids lourd sénégalais s’est imposé par KO technique dès le premier round, renouant ainsi avec le succès après sa défaite d’avril dernier. Lire aussi: MMA : des rues des Parcelles à la Professional Fighters League (PFL) – Abdoulaye Kane, le combat d’une vie Selon les résultats publiés par la Professional Fighters League (PFL), Abdoulaye Kane a mis fin au combat à 4 minutes et 6 secondes du premier round, grâce à un KO technique. Cette performance lui permet de rebondir après son revers concédé face au Britannique Justin Clarke, le 10 avril 2026, à Pretoria, en Afrique du Sud. Cette victoire s’inscrit dans le parcours d’un combattant qui s’est progressivement fait une place sur la scène internationale des arts martiaux mixtes. Né et grandi aux Parcelles Assainies, à Dakar, Abdoulaye Kane a construit son parcours entre petits métiers, séjour au Maroc et pratique du sambo avant de se tourner vers le MMA professionnel, selon un portrait publié par Le Soleil en juillet 2026. Avec cette victoire à Casablanca, le Sénégalais confirme sa capacité à rebondir dans une catégorie où la puissance et l’efficacité peuvent faire basculer un combat en quelques secondes. Son succès face à Badr Medkouri lui permet de reprendre sa marche en avant au sein de la PFL, une organisation qui contribue au développement du MMA sur le continent africain. A.N

items.title: Yet Another Literary Prizewinner Seems to Be AI
items.description: B ecause literary journals tend to have small circulations, few readers are likely to have come across “ The Whistleblower ,” a short story by the Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza. Published in 2021 in a journal called Transition , the story is a taut and closely observed political thriller in miniature. Its narrator, a sharp but inexperienced computer-science graduate in Harare, Zimbabwe, encounters an intelligence officer at the mall—a former teacher of his—who now wants something from him. At first, the graduate is nervous for what turns out to be the wrong reason: “I’d had a brief relationship with his niece Agatha and I wasn’t sure whether he knew about this or how he felt about it if he did.” A more recent story with Kundizeza’s name on it, “ The Blue Fighter ,” will surely find its way to more readers. Last week, it was named the winner of the prestigious Caine Prize for African Writing, which awards 10,000 British pounds (about $13,000) for a short story by an African writer. Some previous winners, including Namwali Serpell and NoViolet Bulawayo , are now among the world’s most celebrated authors. Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad—maudlin and full of tired tropes. Here, the Zimbabwean narrator is the son of a hapless father who squanders the family’s money trying to breed fish in tanks, to the mother’s chagrin. “‘We can’t afford this house anymore,’ she said one evening, placing the notice in front of him while he tested the seal on his newest creation,” the story reads. “Not with anger, but with the quiet resignation of someone who had known all along this moment would come.” At the end, the narrator compares the last remaining fish to his family: “Not broken, just learning how to live differently. Alone, sometimes. But still moving. Still here.” That this narrator has all the personality of a chatbot is probably not coincidental. The AI detector Pangram flags almost the entire story as AI-generated; a notable exception is its epigraph, also about a father with a fish fixation, which is excerpted from what’s described as an unpublished poem by Vangile Gantsho. This isn’t the first prize-winning story to be flagged by Pangram. It comes after similar scandals over this year’s Commonwealth Prize and Prix Goncourt —two other renowned literature contests—in which Pangram flagged AI use among finalists. In the case of the Commonwealth Prize, one of them eventually won ; the Prix Goncourt pulled a writer from consideration after suspected AI use was compounded by plagiarism allegations over his earlier work. Any of these incidents might have been written off as a fluke. Together, they point to something of a crisis of trust—in both writers and technology—that threatens to undermine a global system of literary recognition. [ Read: The literary AI scandal that changes everything ] AI detection is fallible , which has raised concerns among some readers and writers about the prospect of false positives. But Pangram, which uses AI for its classification of text, is highly accurate : The company says its tool mistakenly labels human text as AI in about one in 24,000 cases; outside research also finds false positives to be extremely rare. When I ran all 25 of the previous Caine Prize-winning stories through Pangram, it labeled them as 100 percent human-written; the same is true of Kundizeza’s “The Whistleblower.” I reached out to Kundizeza about Pangram’s assessment of “The Blue Fighter” through his agent, Adrienne Ingrum at the Serendipity Literary Agency. She wrote that Regina Brooks, the agency’s CEO, would send me “evidence that the author and we at Serendipity are completely confident that the story is Simba’s own work.” Neither Ingrum nor Brooks followed up before publication. I also spoke at length with Ellah Wakatama, who chairs the Caine Prize’s board of trustees. Wakatama, a longtime book editor, told me that AI-generated fiction is not eligible for the prize. As soon as she learned of an inquiry I’d sent about the Pangram assessment of Kundizeza’s story, she and her colleagues initiated an investigation and contacted the author. Wakatama told me that she and a colleague will interview the prize judges, and that she’ll reread Kundizeza’s story and talk with him in detail about his methods. She added that a colleague has been in contact with Kundizeza’s agent about whether a verification process might include, say, reviewing previous drafts. Yet Wakatama forcefully rejected the notion that an AI detector could, or should, be used to gauge AI involvement. “My stance, as the person who leads the prize, is that if there is such an accusation, I want proof that does not come from a machine.” She said she planned to approach Kundizeza with “compassion” and the presumption of honesty. Wakatama is also Zimbabwean. “As an African,” she said, “my first stance is, if I ask you, Are you telling the truth? and if you say yes, I am going to believe you—especially because the accusers are not coming from amongst our own people.” Wakatama remarked on details in Kundizeza’s story that strike her as so typically Zimbabwean that a Zimbabwean must have written them: the shame of moving from a nice suburb to a less privileged township; how the mother’s initial forbearance with the father gives way to taking matters into her own hands. Wakatama also perceives multiple layers of meaning. She doesn’t think AI models are capable of that kind of cultural or literary nuance. [ Read: The Pangram backlash unfolding on college campuses ] But then, she acknowledged that she doesn’t use AI or AI detectors. “My first response when somebody asks me to use AI is that I think about water and energy,” she said—that is, AI companies’ excessive use of both. “That honestly overwhelms me, and I don’t want to.” Wakatama isn’t involved in choosing the Caine Prize winner—a panel of judges reads all the submissions—but her approach to AI is common among organizations that award prizes or other honors to writers. Partly, this is a pragmatic response to the risk of false positives. “Our legal parameters don’t allow us to contest the honesty of our writers just because a tool says that,” Razmi Farook, the director-general of the Commonwealth Foundation, told me during the scandal over its prize. But this wariness also reflects a general aversion, in literary and arts circles, to engaging with AI products, even if just to understand them better—including Pangram. The start-up’s product itself is based on AI, and it belongs to the Silicon Valley ecosystem; the company recently raised $50 million in funding, according to a person familiar with the deal. The skepticism is easy to understand, but it might be shortsighted. Research suggests that the people most familiar with AI output excel at sniffing it out. I’ve covered AI for almost a decade, and have written fiction for even longer; in short, I’ve had plenty of exposure to both literature and chatbot output. I know from experience that, for example, AI models aren’t terrible at picking up on cultural details. When I read “The Blue Fighter,” I was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions ; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms. “Anger burns out eventually,” the narrator’s mother says at one point. “Hunger doesn’t.” The earlier story by Kundizeza lacked those stylistic qualities, its prose and dialogue far more plainspoken and natural-sounding: “So how are things with my niece, huh?” the intelligence officer asks at one point. What I also noticed, more disturbingly, was the presence of stereotypes about African life common among outsiders: a blundering, unemployed father; a resilient matriarch who dispenses clichéd approximations of wisdom; an environment of deprivation. Research consistently shows that AI products reproduce cultural tropes , including those having to do with the African continent . [ Read: The most famous AI writing tic is also the most mysterious ] The novelist and critic Tope Folarin , a former Caine Prize winner who has written about how dominant white culture shapes global literature, told me after reading the story that it would be unfortunate if Kundizeza had relied on AI for any of it, because its plot is “deeply human” and “deserves human expression.” He also said, “There are a lot of writers from the global South who feel this extreme pressure to write to expectations so their work is legible to the West, and obviously chatbots have glommed onto that.” He called the incident a “tragedy.” Wakatama, for her part, explained her suspicion of AI detection by referencing the long , fraught history of science being used to oppress people of color. To a skeptical reader, her invocation of race might sound like a preemptive excuse. But in our conversation, she came across as open-minded and intellectually honest. I considered her wariness of Silicon Valley well founded and reasonable—particularly because the writers implicated in three major literary scandals this year were all nonwhite and non-American. Pangram’s internal research finds false positives to be rare or nonexistent across multiple races and languages, as well as for English-language learners writing in English. In a separate peer-reviewed study , researchers at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel found zero false positives for English-language writing by non-native English speakers. It’s also notable that Pangram didn’t detect AI in any previous Caine Prize–winning stories or in a pre-ChatGPT story of Kundizeza’s. Yet third-party research into Pangram’s effectiveness for writers across nationalities is limited. Still, it seems that arts communities’ revulsion toward AI has fostered a self-defeating underinvestment in understanding how exactly it functions, and how those who are repelled by AI companies’ presence in cultural spheres might beat back its encroachment. If an AI-detection tool is known to work really well, couldn’t we at least use it alongside other methods? Barring that, couldn’t we build some expertise in detecting fakery the old-fashioned way—through human training and intuition? “Language carries culture,” the Kenyan novelist Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o once wrote, “and culture carries, particularly through orature and literature, the entire body of values by which we come to perceive ourselves and our place in the world.” Language, he added, is “thus inseparable from ourselves as a community of human beings with a specific form and character, a specific history, a specific relationship to the world.” Ngũgĩ, following this line of reasoning, chose to return to his native language of Gĩkũyũ after having built a career writing in English. That is, he analyzed the situation, and then changed his approach. Maybe the broader artistic community can learn from that. Toward the end of our conversation, Wakatama told me, “I am fervently praying that you’re wrong.” It would be easier if I were wrong; indeed, maybe I am. But if I’m right, it means that several of the world’s most prestigious literary prizes have been infected by language that represents not people’s actual values and cultures but a damaging mimicry of them by products of the most powerful companies and people in the world. This is the time to do something about it.

items.title: Arabie saoudite : 12 morts et 309 blessés dans une attaque contre l’aéroport de Riyad
items.description: Au moins 12 personnes ont été tuées et 309 autres blessées samedi dans une attaque visant l’aéroport international King Khalid de Riyad. La coalition militaire dirigée par l’Arabie saoudite accuse les Houthis du Yémen d’être à l’origine de cette frappe, tandis que les autorités ont suspendu les activités de l’aéroport. L’attaque contre l’aéroport international King Khalid de Riyad a fait au moins 12 morts et 309 blessés, selon les autorités saoudiennes. Parmi les victimes figurent quatre ressortissants saoudiens et huit étrangers, dont un Américain. Le bilan communiqué fait état de quatre Saoudiens, deux Bangladais, un Américain, un Égyptien, un Argentin, un Syrien, un Palestinien et un Soudanais parmi les personnes tuées. Cette attaque est présentée comme la plus meurtrière en Arabie saoudite depuis plus d’une décennie. Le dernier bilan comparable remonte à août 2015, lorsqu’un attentat attribué à l’organisation État islamique avait fait 15 morts dans une mosquée du quartier général des forces spéciales à Abha. La coalition militaire menée par Riyad, qui soutient le gouvernement internationalement reconnu du Yémen, a accusé les Houthis, mouvement soutenu par l’Iran, d’être responsables de l’attaque. Les opérations ont été suspendues à l’aéroport de Riyad. Le ministère saoudien de l’Éducation a également annoncé que les établissements scolaires de la capitale fonctionneraient à distance pendant une semaine. La coalition a par ailleurs annoncé qu’un projectile était tombé à proximité de l’aéroport de Dammam, dans l’est du pays. Cet aéroport, avec celui de Djeddah, constitue une alternative à l’aéroport de Riyad, fermé depuis l’attaque. Un autre projectile aurait été intercepté au sud-est de la capitale. Dans les hôpitaux de Riyad, les médecins ont été appelés en urgence afin de prendre en charge les centaines de blessés. Plusieurs ambassades ont également recommandé à leur personnel d’éviter l’aéroport pendant une semaine, selon un diplomate occidental cité par France 24. The post Arabie saoudite : 12 morts et 309 blessés dans une attaque contre l’aéroport de Riyad appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Governor’s rule and emergency imposed in KP — here’s what it means
items.description: The federal government imposed an emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa amid growing tensions with the PTI-led provincial government, including disagreements over counterterrorism policy amid a deteriorating security situation in the province. The decision was taken under Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution of Pakistan. Here is what it means. Governor’s rule Article 234 of the Constitution of Pakistan stipulates that, if the president believes that a provincial government cannot function in accordance with the Constitution, the federal government can assume control of the province. This can be done either directly or by assigning the relevant functions to the provincial governor — hence the term governor’s rule. Under this arrangement, the powers of the provincial assembly can be exercised by Parliament. However, neither the president nor the governor can assume the powers of the high court or suspend its operations. Moreover, governor’s rule can be imposed for an initial period of two months, with a joint sitting of Parliament able to approve an extension of up to two months at a time. In total, governor’s rule can remain in place for a maximum of six months. While a province is under governor’s rule, its government or the chief minister cannot exercise their powers, but “I don’t see how it brings the government to an end”, said lawyer Mirza Moiz Baig. He added, “The government would come back into existence upon the end of the emergency”. “Once the proclamation expires, the Chief Minister and his Cabinet are restored,” lawyer Rida Hosain told Dawn . State of emergency Meanwhile, under Article 232, which pertains to the proclamation of an emergency, the provincial assembly continues to function as usual. However, if a provincial law conflicts with a federal law enacted by Parliament, the latter takes precedence. Lawyer Basil Nabi Malik, speaking to Dawn , explained that the chief minister would remain in office during a state of emergency. However, the federal government could assume certain functions of the provincial government. An emergency also allows the federal government to make provisions it considers necessary and suspend certain constitutional provisions relating to provincial bodies. However, as with governor’s rule, the federal government cannot assume the powers of a high court. It also empowers Parliament to confer powers and impose duties on federal government officers in the province. It further stipulates that laws passed by Parliament solely on account of the emergency will cease to have effect six months after the emergency ends. The proclamation of emergency lapses after two months unless it is approved by a resolution of a joint sitting of Parliament.

items.title: 2026 World Maritime Day: Danish Embassy organises “The Gulf of Guinea Speaks”
items.description: As part of activities to mark the 2026 World Maritime Day and the 10 th anniversary of the Danish Maritime Security Programme for the Gulf of Guinea, the Royal Danish Embassy Accra presented “The Gulf of Guinea Speaks”, a site‑specific art intervention held at the Ambassador’s Residence in Accra. Under the theme “From Policy to Practice: Powering Maritime Excellence”, three commissioned artworks brought human ‑ centered creative perspectives to the diplomatic maritime‑security discussions. Curated by Fang Wang (Fang W. Linulf) and Essé Dabla‑Attikpo, the show featured Ghanaian artists Patrick Tagoe‑Turkson and Emmanuel Aggrey Tieku alongside a large‑scale floor work by Fang W. Linulf. Tagoe‑Turkson repurposed beach‑collected plastic flip‑flops for mixed‑media assemblages addressing marine waste and coastal heritage. Aggrey Tieku also built monumental installations from salvaged second‑hand textiles to interrogate waste colonialism and global‑trade pollution. Fang’s 100 sqm floor print merges ocean imagery and maritime geographic data, letting visitors physically stand upon mapped Gulf‑of‑Guinea ocean geography. Moving beyond official reports, the art intervention used sensory visual storytelling to highlight ocean ecology, coastal‑community realities and the human side of maritime governance for attending diplomats. Co – curator and artist Fang W. Linulf mentioned that visitors literally walk across the ocean on my floor print whilst abstract maritime data becomes something bodily and immediate. She further stated that “policy builds frameworks for maritime security, yet art uncovers the human and material stories often missing from official documents. We wanted delegates to feel, not only read, the realities of the Gulf of Guinea coast.” Essé Dabla‑Attikpo, also a co‑Curator “The Gulf of Guinea Speaks” stated that “waste arriving on our shores is not just an environmental problem. It carries global trade histories. Through re‑making discarded materials, we give visibility to these hidden narratives.” Patrick Tagoe‑Turkson transformed ocean washed plastic flip‑flops collected from Ghana’s Atlantic shorelines into layered mixed‑media assemblages. At the event, he said that “discarded flip‑flops and textiles washed onto our beaches hold cultural memories. Transforming waste into art is one way to advocate for our ocean and our coastal heritage.” Commenting on the exhibition, Emmanuel Aggrey Tieku mentioned that “I work with second‑hand garments that end up in Ghana’s landfills and beaches. These textiles are physical evidence of waste colonialism and unequal global supply chains.” The “The Gulf of Guinea Speaks” event was attended by maritime practitioners, diplomats and industry stakeholders and created a platform to experience maritime realities through sensory, material and visual perspectives, raising public awareness through artistic practice.

items.title: New Economy will tackle unemployment and restore hope – Ato Forson
items.description: Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson says Ghana’s New Economy will confront the human cost of unemployment and address the barriers preventing young people, farmers and small businesses from building sustainable livelihoods. According to him, the country could no longer accept a situation in which education fails to lead to employment, talent remains unsupported and productive effort yields little opportunity. “Unemployment is personal. It is the graduate who has finished school but cannot find work. It is the young person with talent but no capital,” he said. Dr Forson’s message places jobs and economic opportunity at the centre of the New Economy, drawing attention to the everyday struggles behind unemployment figures. He highlighted the plight of farmers who produce without reliable markets and small business owners whose ambitions to expand are frustrated by the cost of credit. His remarks underscored the need to address both the search for work and the obstacles facing those capable of creating it. For families, he said, the burden is particularly painful after years of sacrifice to finance a child’s education. “It is the family that sacrifices to educate a child, only to watch that child sit at home.” The Finance Minister rejected the idea that such experiences should become an accepted feature of national life. “No serious nation can accept this as normal. The New Economy says Ghana must no longer accept it.” He made these remarks in an engagement with students and faculty of the University of Development Studies at their Nyankpala Campus.

items.title: IMMILAC president recounts personal losses as security women lead breast cancer awareness campaign in Wa
items.description: They usually check passports at the borders. On Friday, they were raising awareness about breast cancer in Wa. Female officers of the Ghana Immigration Service, Ghana Police Service and Ghana Prisons Service took to the principal streets of Wa in a float, dressed in their uniforms and wearing pink ribbons, as they marked Breast Cancer Awareness Month. The exercise turned parts of the Upper West Regional capital pink, drawing attention to the importance of breast cancer awareness, prevention and early detection. Leading the campaign was Deputy Superintendent of Immigration (DSI) Prospera Soliku, President of the Immigration Ladies Association (IMMILAC) in the Upper West Region. In recent years, DSI Soliku has championed the welfare, health and professional development of female officers under her leadership of the association’s regional chapter. Under her presidency, IMMILAC’s annual Pink October campaign has evolved from an internal sensitisation programme for members into a community-wide initiative involving sister security services and the general public. This year’s campaign, however, carried a deeply personal message for the IMMILAC President, who disclosed that she had lost loved ones to breast cancer. “This cause is deeply personal to me. I lost my beloved aunt, who actually cut my wedding cake, as well as a close friend and her sister to this breast cancer,” DSI Soliku told officers at the Regional Headquarters of the Ghana Immigration Service, where the float ended. Held under the theme “Every Story Is Unique, Every Journey Matters,” the exercise sought to raise awareness about breast cancer prevention and the importance of early detection. “October, particularly known as Pink October, is Breast Cancer Awareness Month. Our theme this year reminds us that everyone affected by breast cancer deserves care, compassion, and support,” she said. Beyond the street procession, the campaign focused on educating participants about breast cancer, its risk factors and the importance of seeking medical attention early. Health Promotion Officer at the Wa Municipal Hospital, Leticia Yuorkuu, took participants through the causes, risk factors and prevention of the disease. “Breast cancer is caused by genetic mutation of the DNA. It is inherited or acquired through our lifestyle and environment. It does not spread from person to person either by air, sex, blood or food,” she explained. She identified alcohol consumption, smoking, an unhealthy diet, obesity, lack of exercise, early menarche, late menopause and late childbirth as factors associated with an increased risk of breast cancer. Ms Yuorkuu also addressed a common misconception about breastfeeding and breast cancer prevention. “Suckling by babies can actually help women prevent breast cancer. But sucking by men does not help. Sucking by men is a way of pleasure during sexual activities,” she said, drawing laughter from participants. Medical Officer at the Upper West Regional Hospital, Dr Adam Mansura, cautioned that cancer could spread without obvious symptoms and sought to dispel misconceptions about breast cancer treatment. “Cancer on its own doesn’t cause pain, but that doesn’t mean you cannot have cancer and have pain. That’s why there’s a need to assess and examine. Not every breast cancer treatment leads to removal of the breast. Early detection, early diagnosis saves us. If you are able to detect it early and start your treatment early, you may not have to go through removal,” she stressed. Dr Mansura explained that breast cancer could spread to other parts of the body, including the back, brain, hip, lungs and liver. She also noted that not every breast lump was cancerous. She demonstrated two methods of breast self-examination: using a mirror and examining the breasts while lying on a flat surface. Participants were advised to look out for lumps, changes in breast size or shape, skin discolouration, nipple discharge and other unusual changes in the breasts. At the close of the event, the Regional Commander of the Ghana Immigration Service in the Upper West Region, DCOI Justice Ayensu Bosomtwe, urged officers to take their physical fitness seriously. “You cannot be a security officer and not be fit. When you are called for PT, you don’t expect us to beg you. When persuasion fails, I will do what I feel is right to keep you fit. Because I believe that when we do some of these exercises, at least it will minimise our chances of getting this dreaded disease,” he said. He added that he would enforce physical training as a mandatory parade to encourage officers to exercise regularly. The programme also included free breast screening for participants and members of the public by a medical team from the Upper West Regional Hospital. Those present included the Regional Second-in-Command, the Regional Passport Director, media representatives, officers from sister security services and members of the Immigration Men’s Association, who joined the ladies in supporting the campaign. The organisers stressed the importance of sustaining breast cancer awareness beyond October, encouraging people to prioritise early detection, screening and access to accurate information.

items.title: Trump's diesel deal with Putin: How much, how long, and will It cut prices?
items.description: TEHRAN - On October 9, US President Donald Trump announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply diesel to the US and global markets, paired with a temporary 6-month US sanctions waiver. The move is aimed at easing record-high US diesel prices weeks before the November 3 midterms. Initial volumes are modest relative to consumption, so analysts expect limited and mostly psychological price effects — unless larger follow-on deliveries materialize and Russian refineries recover.

items.title: Profanation du Coran : deux femmes arrêtées à Batna
items.description: Deux femmes suspectées de profanation du Coran ont été arrêtées à Batna, annonce la Sûreté de cette wilaya. Dans un communiqué diffusé ce dimanche 11 octobre sur les réseaux sociaux, la sûreté de wilaya de Batna a indiqué que l’interpellation des deux femmes a fait suite à des informations parvenues à la brigade de lutte contre la cybercriminalité relevant du service de wilaya de la police judiciaire (SWPJ), faisant état d’une vidéo circulant sur les réseaux sociaux et montrant un acte de profanation du livre saint de l’islam. Selon la même source, on peut voir sur la vidéo une femme “posant sa main sur le Coran et jurant sur celui-ci, tout en continuant à proférer des insultes et des blasphèmes sans aucun respect pour le caractère sacré du Coran ”. Batna : arrestation de 2 femmes suspectées de profanation du Coran Après analyse de la vidéo, les agents de la même brigade ont entamé les investigations techniques qui ont permis l’identification et l’arrestation de la suspecte. Il s'agit d’une femme âgée de 51 ans, précise la police. Dans le cadre de la poursuite de l’enquête et en coordination avec le parquet local, sa complice, âgée de 32 ans, a également été interpellée. Après l’accomplissement des procédures légales, les deux suspectes ont été déférées devant le parquet local, ajoute le communiqué qui ne précise pas les dispositions prises par la justice à l'encontre des deux femmes. L’article Profanation du Coran : deux femmes arrêtées à Batna est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Kankan : « Une justice qui tarde ou qui n’écoute pas peut pousser le citoyen à se rendre justice lui-même », alerte le Garde des Sceaux
items.description: À Kankan, le Garde des Sceaux a mis en garde les acteurs judiciaires contre les conséquences des lenteurs dans le traitement des dossiers, des décisions rendues mais non disponibles et du manque d’écoute des justiciables. En visite dans la région, le ministre a annoncé des sanctions contre les responsables qui ne respectent pas leurs obligations. Face aux magistrats et aux responsables des juridictions, le ministre de la Justice et des Droits de l’Homme a rappelé le rôle central de la justice dans le fonctionnement de l’État et la nécessité de la rendre accessible aux citoyens. « Quand la justice marche, tous les autres secteurs suivent. Et si la justice ne marche pas, aucun autre secteur ne peut mieux se comporter », a-t-il déclaré, qualifiant la justice de fondement des autres secteurs. Le Garde des Sceaux a insisté sur l’importance de l’écoute des justiciables, rappelant que ceux qui saisissent les tribunaux ont souvent épuisé d’autres voies pour résoudre leurs différends. « Quand quelqu’un vient vers la justice, c’est parce que quelque part l’intéressé a épuisé toutes les voies de recours. Donc la justice devient son dernier recours », a-t-il expliqué. Pour le ministre, même lorsqu’un justiciable perd son procès, il doit pouvoir constater que sa préoccupation a été examinée et traitée avec considération. Les lenteurs judiciaires dans le viseur Le ministre a particulièrement dénoncé les retards dans le traitement des affaires et la mise à disposition des décisions. Selon lui, laisser un citoyen attendre des mois, voire des années, sans obtenir de réponse judiciaire risque d’alimenter sa frustration et de l’amener à envisager de se faire justice lui-même. « Quelqu’un qui vient à la justice et qui n’est pas écouté, comprenez immédiatement que cette personne va immédiatement penser à se rendre justice. Et là interviendra maintenant une justice privée », a-t-il averti. Il a également rappelé que la justice est rendue au nom du peuple de Guinée et que les magistrats ne peuvent exercer leurs fonctions selon leur seule volonté. « Sachez surtout que la justice est rendue au nom du peuple de Guinée. La justice n’est pas rendue pour le juge », a-t-il martelé. Des décisions rendues, mais parfois indisponibles Autre dysfonctionnement dénoncé : le retard dans la rédaction des décisions et la remise de leurs copies aux parties concernées. Le Garde des Sceaux a regretté que des justiciables soient contraints de courir derrière des décisions pourtant déjà prononcées. « Le juge prend sa décision, il ne rédige pas, les parties courent derrière la décision pendant des mois. À quoi ça sert cette décision ? À rien », a-t-il déploré. Il a rappelé que le travail judiciaire ne s’arrête pas au prononcé d’un jugement. Les responsables des juridictions doivent également veiller à ce que les décisions soient disponibles et que leur exécution soit suivie. « Vous ne devez pas vous contenter de dire : on a rendu la décision et puis c’est fini. Vous devez suivre. Vous devez savoir : est-ce que la décision a été exécutée ? », a-t-il demandé aux responsables judiciaires. Le ministre a par ailleurs insisté sur le respect des exigences procédurales concernant la rédaction des décisions civiles et pénales. Il a notamment affirmé qu’en matière pénale, une décision devrait être prête après trois jours, tout en déplorant les retards observés dans certaines juridictions. « On va commencer à sévir » Face à ces pratiques, le Garde des Sceaux a annoncé son intention de sanctionner les manquements relevant de ses prérogatives. « On va commencer à sévir pour ça. On va commencer à sévir parce que j’ai la prérogative de sanctionner en la matière et je ne vais pas m’empêcher de le faire », a-t-il prévenu. Il a appelé les chefs de juridiction, les procureurs et les responsables de l’inspection judiciaire à assurer le suivi des instructions et à veiller à l’amélioration du fonctionnement des services. Le ministre a toutefois reconnu que certaines procédures nécessitent davantage de temps en raison de contraintes particulières. Il a demandé aux acteurs judiciaires de distinguer ces dossiers de ceux qui peuvent être traités plus rapidement. À Kankan, son message aux acteurs de la justice porte ainsi sur plusieurs exigences : écouter les citoyens, accélérer le traitement des affaires lorsque cela est possible, rendre les décisions accessibles et veiller à leur exécution. L’objectif affiché est de renforcer la confiance des justiciables dans l’institution judiciaire et de prévenir les situations susceptibles de favoriser le recours à la justice privée. Karifa Kansan Doumbouya L’article Kankan : « Une justice qui tarde ou qui n’écoute pas peut pousser le citoyen à se rendre justice lui-même », alerte le Garde des Sceaux est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: University of Ghana postpones October 12 reopening as GAUA strike persists
items.description: The University of Ghana has postponed its reopening for the 2026/2027 academic year, initially scheduled for Monday, October 12, 2026. In a notice dated October 10, 2026, management said a revised reopening date would be announced in due course. The notice did not state the reason for the postponement. However, the postponement comes amid an ongoing strike by the Ghana Association of University Administrators (GAUA), which has affected the effective operation and administration of public universities. The announcement was signed by Prof Gordon A. Awandare, Pro Vice-Chancellor in charge of Academic and Student Affairs. “Management sincerely regrets any inconvenience this postponement may cause and appreciates the patience and understanding of students as arrangements are made for the reopening,” the notice stated. Despite the postponement, students have been urged to complete their academic registration online, following the procedure outlined in the university’s previous communication. Management said completing registration would secure students’ places for classes and ensure their eligibility to participate in the random bed allocation exercise, which is expected to take place soon. Read Also: KNUST postpones 2026/2027 academic year reopening indefinitely amid GAUA strike Before the University of Ghana, the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) also announced a postponement of the reopening of the 2026/2027 academic year indefinitely specifically due to the strike.

items.description: Le Sénégal condamne avec fermeté l’attaque perpétrée le 10 octobre 2026 contre l’aéroport international King Khaled de Riyad, en Arabie saoudite.
