items.title: Miss Littérature Sénégal : dix candidates en lice pour la finale du 14 novembre
items.description: La deuxième édition de Miss Littérature Sénégal connaît ses dix finalistes. À l’issue de la demi-finale organisée le samedi 10 octobre 2026, au Complexe culturel Léopold Sédar Senghor de Pikine, dix candidates ont décroché leur ticket pour la grande finale, prévue le 14 novembre prochain à l’Institut français de Dakar. La compétition entre dans sa dernière ligne droite. Lancée pour promouvoir le livre, la lecture et l’excellence intellectuelle féminine, Miss Littérature Sénégal entend également mettre en lumière les jeunes talents littéraires du pays. Elles étaient en lice pour franchir cette étape décisive. Au terme de la demi-finale, dix candidates ont été retenues pour poursuivre l’aventure. Il s’agit de Khadidiatou Kane, Fatou Binetou Sène, Aïcha Rose Niassy, Mame Mbayame Niang, Dieynaba Bâ, Niama Boumaré, Aïda Bâ, Sophie Charlene Nasala, Fatoumata Diagne et Ndeye Ndiaye. La finale, prévue le 14 novembre 2026 à l’Institut français de Dakar, constituera la dernière étape de cette deuxième édition. Les candidates auront l’occasion d’y défendre leur parcours et leur engagement en faveur de la littérature. À travers cette initiative, le comité d’organisation, dirigé par Salamata Ousmane Diallo, réaffirme son ambition de faire de la lecture et de la culture des leviers d’épanouissement et de valorisation du potentiel intellectuel féminin. Au-delà du concours, Miss Littérature Sénégal entend contribuer au rayonnement de la littérature sénégalaise et encourager les jeunes femmes à investir davantage l’univers du livre. A.N

items.title: ‎Initiative presidentielle pour la relève et la promotion de l’élite sportive : L’Ambassadeur pour le sport joue la carte de la Ligue de l’Espoir (LIDE)
items.description: Le stade Wobi de Bobo-Dioulasso a abrité samedi 10 octobre, le lancement officiel de la première édition de la Ligue de l’Espoir (LIDE). Portée par l'Ambassadeur pour le Sport, le Camarade Charles KABORÉ, ancien capitaine des Étalons, cette compétition, réservée aux moins de 17 ans (U17), s’inscrit dans la vision du Chef de l’État, le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ, à travers l’Initiative Présidentielle pour la Relève et la Promotion de l’Élite Sportive. Le Ministre Secrétaire Général du Gouvernement, le Camarade Ousmane OUATTARA, représentant le Premier ministre, Patron de cette édition, a, dans son discours, relevé le rôle cardinal de la jeunesse dans la Révolution Progressiste Populaire : « Le Chef de l'État, le Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ, place la jeunesse au cœur de la transformation nationale (…) Investir dans la jeunesse, c'est préparer l'avenir de la Nation. Structurer le sport à la base, c'est donner à cette jeunesse des fondations solides pour bâtir l'avenir ». Selon l'Ambassadeur pour le Sport, le Camarade Charles KABORÉ, ce championnat représente une opportunité majeure d'expression et de visibilité pour les jeunes de 13 à 17 ans. « C’est une initiative très importante pour la jeunesse sportive et la promotion de nos compétences (…) Cette compétition offre une opportunité aux jeunes d’être détectés par de grands clubs nationaux et étrangers », a-t-il souligné. Au-delà des aspects compétitifs, avec ce projet ambitieux et s'appuyant sur son expérience, il s'agit pour l'ancien capitaine des Étalons, de transmettre les exigences du milieu professionnel aux plus jeunes. « On veut créer ce cadre-là pour qu'ils soient régulièrement en compétition, comme nous, on l'a été dans le temps. (…) Aujourd'hui nous venons traduire cette expérience ici avec l'accompagnement du Camarade Président, Capitaine Ibrahim TRAORÉ », a expliqué l’Ambassadeur pour le Sport. Cette édition de la LIDE réunit 16 formations réparties entre Bobo-Dioulasso et Ouagadougou, et pose les bases d’un renouveau du football national. Elle ambitionne de devenir un pilier durable du développement du football burkinabè. C'est une initiative qui est mise en œuvre en attendant la Ligue de la Souveraineté, annoncée à l'issue du Conseil des ministres du jeudi dernier avec une plus large ouverture en termes de catégories et une envergure nationale prenant en compte toutes les régions du pays. Le match inaugural de cette première édition de la Ligue de l’Espoir a vu la victoire des U17 de Rahimo FC sur ceux de Vitesse FC par 3 buts à 2. ‎Direction de la communication de la Présidence du Faso

items.title: La consommation de la grenade est bonne pour le cœur
items.description: La production tunisienne de grenades pour la saison 2026 est estimée à 98 000 tonnes, en hausse de 8 % par rapport aux 91 000 tonnes récoltées en 2025, selon les données du Groupement interprofessionnel des fruits (GIFruits). Ç a tombe bien, puisque, selon Dr Faouzi Addad, la consommation de ce fruit qui mûrit en pareille saison de l’année est excellente pour la santé et pourrait même contribuer à diminuer la pression artérielle. «S’il y a un fruit à mettre à l’honneur durant cette période, c’est bien la grenade (dite la pomme de Carthage). Ses petits grains rouges renferment des fibres et une remarquable diversité de polyphénols, notamment des anthocyanes. La grenade contient également des punicalagines, des composés étudiés pour leurs propriétés antioxydantes et anti-inflammatoires» , écrit le professeur en cardiologie dans un post sur sa page Facebook, où il conseille la consommation de la grenade, de préférence sous forme de jus. Pourquoi la grenade intéresse-t-elle les cardiologues ? Réponse du Pr Addad dans le même post: «Plusieurs études suggèrent des effets favorables sur certains marqueurs du stress oxydatif et de l’inflammation, deux mécanismes impliqués dans les maladies cardiovasculaires et dans la rigidité artérielle.» Il ajoute : «Sa consommation, surtout étudiée sous forme de jus, pourrait aussi contribuer à diminuer la pression artérielle. Les résultats sont encourageants, même s’ils varient beaucoup d’une étude à l’autre.» Bien entendu la consommation de la grenade ne fait disparaître les plaques d’athérosclérose ni ne remplace les traitements. «Son intérêt est de trouver sa place dans une alimentation favorable à notre santé» , précise Pr Addad, qui conseille à ses patients de profiter de la saison pour consommer les grains de grenade,qu’il qualifie de «meilleur alliée pour votre cœur et vos artères» . Il conseille, également, de la consommer «nature et sans sucre ajouté, plutôt que de grands verres de jus (riche en sucre)» , afin de conserver les fibres. «En salade ou avec un yaourt nature, elle apportera couleur, saveur et variété à votre assiette» , conclut-il, comme pour vous mettre de l’eau à l bouche. I. B. L’article La consommation de la grenade est bonne pour le cœur est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Techiman unites against child marriage: Joy Impact Makers Awardee leads charge on International Day of the Girl Child
items.description: The Bamiri Community Centre in Techiman in the Bono East Region came alive with energy and purpose as hundreds of schoolgirls, community leaders, and key stakeholders gathered to commemorate this year’s International Day of the Girl Child. The event, organised by the Techiman Municipal Girl Child Coordinator, Mrs Ellen White Opoku, in partnership with the Ghana Education Service (GES), ActionAid Ghana, and other stakeholders, was held under the theme, “End Child Marriage and Invest in Girls’ Rights.” For Mrs Opoku, who also doubles as a 2024 Joy Impact Makers Awardee, this year’s commemoration was yet another testament to her unwavering dedication to championing the rights of the girl child in the Techiman Municipality and beyond. A Recognised Champion for the Girl Child Mrs Ellen White Opoku’s recognition as a 2024 Joy Impact Makers Awardee speaks volumes about her tireless efforts to create a safer and more equitable environment for girls. Her consistent partnership with GES, ActionAid Ghana, and other stakeholders for the umpteenth time demonstrates her commitment to ensuring that the girl child’s voice is heard and her rights are protected. Speaking to JoyNews , Madam Opoku explained the rationale behind this year’s theme, emphasising the urgent need for collective action. “With cases of child marriage recorded in the area, there’s a need for stakeholders to come together to advocate against this canker,” she stated. Her leadership has been instrumental in bringing together diverse stakeholders to confront the challenges facing girls in the municipality. A Unified Front Against Child Marriage The event drew an impressive array of personalities, including the Presiding Judge of the Techiman Circuit Court, Her Worship Sandra Xorlali Lavison, who served as the Special Guest of Honour. Also in attendance were the Member of Parliament for Techiman South, Martin Adjei Mensah Korsah, respected Queen mothers, and hundreds of girls selected from basic and senior high schools across the municipality. The gathering symbolised a united front against child marriage, with each stakeholder bringing their unique influence and perspective to the table. The Law Speaks: Child Marriage is a Crime Her Worship Sandra Xorlali Lavison delivered a powerful legal perspective on the issue, reminding attendees that child marriage is not just a social ill but a criminal offence. “Section 14 of the Children’s Act specifically speaks against child marriage,” she revealed. “Section 15 of the Act speaks about the criminality of giving a child out for marriage, which could end one in prison or a fine.” Her remarks served as a stern warning to anyone considering giving their underage daughter out in marriage, reinforcing that the law is firmly on the side of the girl child. Traditional Leaders Condemn Irresponsible Parenting Nana Ama Asantewaa Munufie II, the Hansuahemaa and Baamuhemaa of the Techiman Traditional Council, who is herself an advocate against child marriage, expressed bewilderment at how parents could give their young daughters away in marriage. “I wonder how parents will give their 12, 13, and 14-year-old girls to marriage,” she questioned, attributing the practice to irresponsible parenting. Her words resonated with many in attendance, highlighting the critical role families play in protecting the rights of the girl child. Education First: A Message to the Girls The Member of Parliament for Techiman South, Martin Adjei Mensah Korsah, used the platform to urge the participating girls to remain focused on their education. “Focus on your education and not on marriages,” he advised. “It would affect their lives negatively.” He encouraged the girls to envision themselves as future leaders, professionals, and change-makers, reminding them that their dreams are valid and achievable through education. He is also calling for tougher punishments for parents found guilty of giving their children away for marriage. ActionAid Ghana Calls for Stronger Measures For ActionAid Ghana, the Regional Programs Manager, Kwame Afram Denkyira, underscored the need for more robust interventions to end child marriage and school-related abuses. “We need stronger measures to end child marriage and school-related abuses,” he called. His appeal reinforced ActionAid’s continued commitment to promoting and protecting the rights of the girl child across Ghana. A Day of Empowerment and Hope The program was not just about speeches and declarations—it was about empowering the hundreds of girls who participated. They left the Bamiri Community Centre with a renewed sense of purpose, armed with knowledge about their rights and the laws that protect them. The event served as a powerful reminder that ending child marriage requires a collective effort from all sectors of society—law enforcement, traditional authorities, educators, parents, and the girls themselves. As the fight against child marriage continues, the Techiman Municipality has sent a clear message: the girl child belongs in the classroom, not in a marital home. Her rights must be protected, and her future must be secured. About Mrs Ellen White Opoku Mrs Ellen White Opoku is the Techiman Municipal Girl Child Coordinator and a 2024 Joy Impact Makers Awardee. Her recognition by JoyNews celebrates her outstanding contributions to the empowerment and protection of the girl child in Ghana. Through her consistent partnership with GES, ActionAid Ghana, and other stakeholders, she continues to be a beacon of hope for countless girls in the Techiman Municipality.

items.title: Ouagadougou : Un artiste musicien condamné à 60 mois de prison pour tentative cambriolage
items.description: Jugé le lundi 5 octobre 2026 devant la chambre correctionnelle du Tribunal de grande instance de Ouaga I pour une tentative de cambriolage commise dans la nuit du 19 au 20 août dernier, un artiste musicien de 25 ans a été reconnu coupable de tentative de vol. Selon les éléments d'audience rapportés par le média spécialisé Justice Infos Burkina , le prévenu, surpris dans un magasin d'ordinateurs qu'il avait forcé à l'aide d'un marteau, a été condamné à une peine de cinq ans de prison, dont six mois ferme, et à une amende de 500 000 FCFA. Les faits se sont déroulés dans la nuit du 19 au 20 août 2026, aux environs de 2 heures du matin. Profitant de la fermeture des commerces et de l'obscurité, Abdoul (nom d’emprunt), un artiste musicien âgé de 25 ans, a ciblé une boutique de vente de matériel informatique. Pour s'introduire à l'intérieur, le jeune homme a arraché une fenêtre en s'aidant d'un marteau que lui avait remis un ami. À la barre de la chambre correctionnelle du Tribunal de grande instance de Ouaga I, lors de l'audience du lundi 5 octobre 2026, le prévenu a reconnu sans détour l'intégralité des faits qui lui sont reprochés. La tentative d'effraction a cependant été interrompue de façon inattendue. Le commerçant propriétaire des lieux, repassant devant son magasin vers 2 heures du matin, a été intrigué par des bruits suspects à l'intérieur. En vérifiant, il a découvert le prévenu dans le local et a tenté de le maîtriser. Une altercation physique s'est ensuivie, au cours de laquelle Abdoul a sorti un coupe-ongles. Pris de panique face à cet objet, le commerçant s'est enfui en poussant des cris d'alerte, ce qui a immédiatement mobilisé les riverains et permis l'interpellation du suspect. Devant les juges, le prévenu a affirmé avoir sorti cet ustensile uniquement pour se dégager alors que la victime le tenait à la gorge. Comme l'indique la relation des débats publiée par Justice Infos Burkina , le ministère public a estimé la culpabilité du prévenu parfaitement établie au regard des aveux constants faits au commissariat puis devant le parquet. Le procureur avait initialement requis une peine de 60 mois d’emprisonnement, dont 24 mois ferme, assortie d'une amende de 2 000 000 FCFA. Bien que le prévenu ait sollicité la clémence de la cour en plaidant une première infraction et en promettant de ne plus recommencer, le tribunal l'a déclaré coupable. En délibéré contradictoire, les juges l'ont condamné à 60 mois d’emprisonnement, dont six mois ferme , ainsi qu'à une amende ferme de 500 000 FCFA . items.title: A Left-Wing Politics Based on Calling People Names
items.description: Among the many areas of American life democratized by the internet, few have been more transformed than political commentary. Instead of being restricted to an old boys’ club of op-ed writers and Sunday-talk-show guests, punditry is now open to anyone with an internet connection. This shift has created abundant opportunities for once-neglected voices and broadened public discourse beyond a narrow establishment-media consensus. But lowering the barrier to entry has also had its downsides, mainly in the rise of political influencers. Like talk-radio hosts of yore, charismatic social-media commentators are skilled at forming a personal relationship with their listeners. Many of the most successful, however, pay next to zero attention to the details of policy or governance and gain followers mostly by calling the other side names. Consider the case of Jennifer Welch, author of the new book Not Today, Fascists . A co-host of the left-wing podcast I’ve Had It , Welch commands millions of followers across Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and other platforms. Multiple times a week, she delights her legions of fans by mocking Donald Trump, whom she calls “America’s dumbass dictator,” and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, whom she derides as “Chuckles,” for his insufficiently ardent resistance to the “fascist” GOP. She has called Erika Kirk, the widow of the murdered conservative activist Charlie Kirk, an “absolute grifter,” and the MAGA movement an “anti-family, pro-pedophilia death cult.” Her response to Lindsey Graham’s death was to say, “He liked cock, as we all know.” (No, we don’t. No evidence that the bachelor senator was gay has ever surfaced .) To people who do not already share her politics, Welch’s coarseness can be off-putting. But it clearly has a cathartic appeal for many disillusioned liberals. Ironically, a major component of Welch’s appeal is inspired by the man she so despises. “I disagree with everything he says, I think he’s a compulsive liar, et cetera,” Welch told National Public Radio last year, “but the way we talk is really the way Trump has been doing it the last 10 years.” [ Read: Megyn Kelly’s extreme makeover ] As a rule, when a book of political commentary has a big picture of the author on the front cover, readers should expect little substance and a lot of righteous certainty. Not Today, Fascists is no exception. But Welch’s rise as a progressive influencer, the growing popularity of her rhetorical style, and the leftward pressure she and her followers are putting on the Democratic Party exemplify a larger current: The American left has decided to mimic the right by cocooning itself in its own echo chamber. “The Democratic base has abandoned traditional media,” Welch writes, “just like the Republican base did ten years ago, and they are desperate for something that goes against the status quo.” This “hunger for something different” among progressives, she observes, has been “so immense that a 51-year-old interior designer and her divorce lawyer started a podcast in Oklahoma a little over three years ago, and it’s now one of the top left-leaning podcasts in the country.” During Trump’s first term, Welch, a successful interior decorator, starred in the Bravo reality-television series Sweet Home Oklahoma . Inspired by the voyeurism of the Real Housewives franchise, the show followed the exploits of Welch and her wealthy friends through the physical and mental landscape of Nichols Hills, her fashionable Oklahoma City neighborhood. Typical plotlines involved Welch’s design business, her husband’s recovery from drug addiction, and a character going on her first blind date in many years. After two seasons, the show was canceled in 2018. Four years later, Welch started I’ve Had It with one of her former co-stars, Angie Sullivan, as a sidekick. According to The New York Times , the podcast initially consisted of “banter about petty grievances.” Gradually, the grievances became political and “grew to world-historical proportions.” Today, I’ve Had It is a go-to stop for Democratic presidential aspirants and other stars of the progressive firmament. Welch has appeared on The View , The New Yorker Radio Hour (interviewed by the magazine’s editor, David Remnick), and the livestream of fellow leftist shock-jock Hasan Piker , who refers to her as “one of the leaders of the radical wine-mom brigade.” Today, the Times reports, Welch “releases a podcast episode approximately once every seven hours.” [ Read: Why Democrats are losing the culture war ] Welch has become the quintessential #resistance influencer—someone animated by righteous indignation over Donald Trump’s misogyny and other character defects. She is Howard Beale crossed with Martha Stewart. Reading her is like being subjected to MS NOW on full volume, but with F-bombs. Indeed, the progressive cable-news network, formerly known as MSNBC, isn’t left-wing enough for Welch, who writes that “I’ve moved left and weaned myself off corporate news in recent years.” To the extent that Not Today, Fascists has a thesis, it’s that Republicans are an assemblage of fascists, pedophiles, and idiots—and that progressives must sink to their level in order to win. “The only way forward is to fight fair,” Welch writes, “which in this case means dirty as hell.” What Democrats need is a “fuck you politics,” she believes. Practically, this means using meaner, cruder language. “If any chickenshit pearl-clutchers gets their panties in a wad because we call Trump a fascist or a Nazi, step aside and let the grown-ups fight,” Welch writes. “Fuck the seniority system. Fuck compromise.” Never in Not Today, Fascists does Welch express the slightest scintilla of a doubt about anything she believes. She cannot contemplate the possibility that others might disagree with her in good faith, without racist, venal, or otherwise malign motives. Like many partisans before her, she implies that voters’ failure to adopt her side’s preferred policies is because the other side has brainwashed them. “We have an uphill battle when it comes to the economy—not because the Democrats’ policies are weaker, but because the propaganda has been so successful,” she writes. The argument that Republican voters foolishly vote against their own economic interests was most famously elucidated in Thomas Frank’s 2004 book, What’s the Matter With Kansas , the thesis of which is that the GOP wages the culture war to distract working-class white voters from its plundering of the economy. “Democratic politicians and candidates should be on TV every single day, beating the drum against corporate America’s exploitations, its billionaire CEOs, and the system that has enabled them to steal from America—and they should do so using clear, aggressive language,” Welch writes, as if such points haven’t been a staple of Democratic rhetoric for decades. As an example of Democratic fecklessness, Welch points to the failure of the Biden administration to have Trump convicted for his role in the January 6 insurrection. She ridicules former Attorney General Merrick Garland for proceeding “as though he’d overdone it on the Xanax.” That Garland might have been at least partly justified in wanting to avoid the appearance of partisanship, a caution he demonstrated by first bringing cases against hundreds of rioters, is lost on Welch. The Biden administration’s attorney general “should have been vetted to make sure he or she understood the assignment,” which, apparently, was not conducting a fair and thorough investigation, but prosecuting Trump and his allies. [ David A. Graham: Donald Trump gets away with it ] This disregard for due process—for the idea that Garland’s long service in the American judicial system might have informed his prosecutorial restraint—is especially startling for someone flinging accusations of “fascism” onto anyone and anything she doesn’t like. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is “no different, in my eyes, from Hitler’s Gestapo,” she writes. A message from the State Department announcing a pause in the issuance of immigrant visas to citizens of 75 countries “isn’t language reminiscent of fascism—it’s obviously and explicitly fascist.” Not Today, Fascists is a sloppy book. It’s riddled with malapropisms (Adolf Hitler sought to “coalesce momentum for World War II”), clichés (“it takes a village”), mixed metaphors (the establishment’s supposed belief that the rich are “the smartest people on God’s green Earth,” when in reality “they are not, uniformly, the brightest of bulbs”), and non sequiturs (“Note that to the MAGA cult, gay sex includes simply existing as a trans person.”) “Books are not known for coming together quickly,” Welch writes. This one certainly seems like it did. But the bigger problem with the book is her uncritical recitation of left-wing talking points. Welch employs one of the most tiresome progressive rhetorical tics, referring frequently to the Trump administration as “the regime.” She calls the extensively documented scandal involving Somali immigrants running fake day-care centers in Minnesota “an utterly fraudulent accusation.” Welch repeats a laundry list of progressive shibboleths from the past decade: that Trump referred to the Nazis and white supremacists at Charlottesville as “very fine people,” that Trump labeled immigrants generally—not just participants in criminal activity—as “animals.” She brings no more reflection or nuance to her discussion of the war in Gaza. “I will not go to great lengths to argue that a genocide is in place, because the reality is clear,” she writes. (In other words, she barely bothers to justify the grave claim she makes.) Welch admits that she “didn’t know much about” the Israeli-Palestinian conflict until well into the current war. She begins the first of her two chapters about the conflict, entitled “Taxpayer-Funded Genocide,” with a memory of her visit to Dachau at the age of 16. The message seems to be that Jews have forgotten what the Nazis did to them and are callously inflicting the same horrors upon Palestinians. Welch claims that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu “has made Jewish people less safe worldwide,” and favorably cites a writer who claims that Israel is “the world’s most powerful cause of antisemitism.” The implication that Jews everywhere are a natural target for opponents of Israeli policy rationalizes bigotry and absolves the actual anti-Semites of their crimes. At one point in Not Today, Fascists , Welch begins to rant about the evils of “Zionist American billionaires” and the “growing Zionist cooperation and Zionist power in the American government.” A commentator more steeped in the history of real-life fascism might be warier of tropes about Jews manipulating the levers of power. Welch’s political consciousness was heavily shaped by her experience growing up in a proudly atheist household surrounded by conservative evangelical Christians. ( Not Today, Fascists is dedicated “To all the blue dots in red states: You’re not crazy—they are.”) Her feelings about the American religious right—which overwhelmingly supports Israel—and her domestic political commitments more broadly seem to color her feelings about the Jewish state. “One striking fact” about the Trump era, she writes, is that “Netanyahu was delighted by Trump. I found it repulsive that he went to Mar-a-Lago to kiss the ring.” One can find Netanyahu’s obsequiousness toward Trump unseemly while simultaneously accepting that foreign leaders, just to do their job, must constantly flatter the most powerful man in the world. One can also abhor the actions of the Israeli government without writing off the entire country as an illegitimate enterprise. By their nature, “heterodox” voices are an acquired taste. In the part of the political universe Welch inhabits, the battle lines are clear: Protect your friends and villainize your opponents, regardless of the details. Discussing the murder of the health-care executive Brian Thompson, she writes that his death “illuminated a harsh reality about American life: The unconscionable cruelty of the American healthcare system has driven some people so far into desperation and despair that they couldn’t find any empathy for the CEO.” That may be true for a radical fringe, but 82 percent of Americans are satisfied with their health-care coverage. In a paean to Tim Walz, Welch describes the Minnesota governor and failed vice-presidential candidate as “the hard-ass you could go to for counsel, who stood up for the underdog like the great American film heroes we grew up watching.” There are many things one can say about Tim Walz; that he is the latter-day incarnation of Paul Newman or Harrison Ford is not one of them. There is a place for the Jennifer Welches of the world, just as there is a place for the Tucker Carlsons and Hasan Pikers and Sean Hannitys. Unabashed partisanship helps motivate some people to win elections. What makes sharply partisan media figures so useful to political movements, however, is precisely what renders them so uninteresting as thinkers. In an earlier era of political commentary, William F. Buckley Jr. earned cachet with his friendships across the political aisle; part of what made him interesting was his interest in other people and their ideas. A typical episode of Firing Line —his current-affairs debate show, which aired on public television for 33 years—would feature Buckley in spirited, respectful conversation with a guest such as Huey Newton, Allen Ginsberg, or John Kenneth Galbraith. Welch and her listeners, by contrast, have no interest in anyone outside their ideological bubble, other than as targets of invective. [ Read: The Hasan Piker question ] In encouraging her fellow progressives to follow MAGA into the gutter, Welch resembles that which she hates. At one point, she writes that “the feeling of being united against a common enemy, with total absolution from racism, sexism, or accountability, can be intoxicating.” But Welch and her followers too are in desperate need of an intervention. Like her adversaries, Welch long ago gave up trying to convince those who don’t see things her way. “I don’t imagine a world where MAGA voters will wake up one morning and simply switch sides,” she writes. Democrats must therefore move left; on this, “there is no compromise” to be had. The Democratic Party is up for grabs, and Jennifer Welch may very well represent its future.

items.title: All the Things You’re Not Allowed to Say In Texas
items.description: Updated at 12:13 p.m. ET on October 11, 2026 S ara Spurgeon , an English professor at Texas Tech University in Lubbock, has been teaching literature for 20 years. But preparing for the spring 2026 semester was the first time she was forced to submit her course materials through a portal to be evaluated by an artificial-intelligence program. It flags anything that might violate new rules laid out by the university chancellor, including a prohibition on the “advocacy/promotion of race or sex-based prejudice,” and a requirement—now Texas state law—that “only two sexes, male and female, are recognized.” At Texas Tech, medical students no longer learn about racial disparities in medical care. Faculty at the university’s medical center in Lubbock were advised to “refrain from treating transgender patients, for any medical condition, if a medical student was present,” according to a lawsuit filed by the American Association of University Professors. (When asked for comment, a spokesperson said that the university’s “written guidance is publicly available and expressly protects instruction necessary for licensure and patient care.”) According to the same lawsuit, the censorship bot—officially known as the Course Content Review Process—ordered a Tech philosophy professor to remove Plato’s Republic from a syllabus because “it references Plato’s beliefs concerning gender roles and homosexuality.” Professors in the Texas A&M system have had to strip their syllabi too. According to an ACLU lawsuit , last January, Aaron George, a professor at Tarleton State University, was told by administrators to remove A Gay Manifesto , a Stonewall-era LGBTQ-rights pamphlet, and White Flight , a history of urban segregation, from his American-political-history course. After a student complained that a different class the professor taught violated university policy, George was informed by administrators that it would be canceled if he did not make “necessary” (but unspecified) changes. He cut a reference in the course description to the significance of the Fourteenth Amendment for LGBTQ rights, and the class was allowed to proceed. The University of Texas at Austin, the flagship school of the UT system, announced last month that it was eliminating majors in Africana studies, Mexican American and Latino studies, women’s and gender studies, and race and migration studies. More than 100 courses have been flagged for removal from the core curriculum, primarily ones relating to slavery, race, gender, sexuality, and the environment. Consolidating majors isn’t necessarily nefarious, nor is rethinking a core curriculum (a central group of courses from which students must take a certain number to graduate). But these changes are happening, Lauren Gutterman, an American studies professor at UT, told me, “entirely because of the political context.” [ Adam Kirsch: Texas sends Plato back to his cave ] The changes to Texas public-university systems are being presented as a necessary corrective to left-wing orthodoxy on campus. Over the past decade, many Americans have come to believe that academia is too ideological and too intolerant of conservative views and arguments. Censoriousness is not an exclusively left-wing phenomenon, but it is real. And some conservative speakers on college campuses met with protests that, while themselves a form of speech, occasionally deteriorated into violence . “Our nation is witnessing a merciless campaign to wipe out our history, defame our heroes, erase our values, and indoctrinate our children,” President Trump declared in 2019 . “One of their political weapons is ‘Cancel Culture’—driving people from their jobs, shaming dissenters, and demanding total submission from anyone who disagrees. This is the very definition of totalitarianism, and it is completely alien to our culture and our values.” Perhaps it’s less alien than Trump supposed. In the name of fighting propaganda and indoctrination, Texan politicians have established strict state controls on what can be taught, researched, and even discussed in the classroom. However bad left-wing censoriousness is or was, the Republican response in Texas has been to ensure that what is taught in the state’s universities is itself propaganda and indoctrination. Ellen Schrecker, a historian of McCarthyism at Yeshiva University, told me that this campaign goes beyond even the repression of the McCarthy era, when censorship led to firings and purges but the government did not interfere directly with what students were taught. After all, American politicians understood that there was a Cold War to win, and that it could not be won if the universities themselves were destroyed. By outlawing or banning forms of speech and inquiry, and by eliminating faculty independence, today’s Republicans are doing much more damage. Texas passed the first of its education gag laws in 2021 to limit the teaching of “critical race theory” in K–12 classrooms. Texas also tried to ban books dealing with racism or LGBTQ themes from public and school libraries; lawmakers characterized the latter as “pornography.” In 2023, the legislature banned “diversity, equity, and inclusion” in higher education, leading to the closure of DEI offices at state-funded institutions. Last year, Texas passed Senate Bill 37 to sharply curtail shared governance—the process by which faculty, administrators, and boards collaborate in running universities; this left political appointees and administrators with unchecked power over hiring and curricula. Governor Greg Abbott had bragged about signing a free-speech law in 2019. Following pro-Palestinian protests on Texas campuses in 2023, he signed a new law banning “expressive activities” from 10 p.m. to 8 a.m., and allowing schools to forbid student protests in some public areas. The seven Texas public-university systems serve more than 700,000 students—several times the enrollment of all Ivy League institutions combined. There are many ways to destroy a university. Texas Tech, Texas A&M, and the University of Texas have each taken a different approach to enforcing the new state laws, with varying degrees of heavy-handedness. But the result will be the same: substandard education, substandard research, and graduates who are less prepared for their future as workers, thinkers, and citizens, and more prepared to obey without question. T exas Tech’s approach to censorship is notable for being both onerous and clumsy, in part because it relies so heavily on artificial intelligence. Curriculum review traditionally involved faculty, administrators, department chairs, and deans who offered expert input without subjecting teaching decisions to the whims of trustees or politicians who might have political or economic interests in avoiding certain subjects. The process still involves layers of review from administrators and university leaders, but the faculty’s role has been replaced in part by the censorship bot, which scans course materials considered potentially controversial. Asked about the role of AI, a spokesperson for the university said that “the Course Content Review process will continue to be faculty-led, just as it was designed to be from the beginning.” Texas Tech’s new chancellor, Brandon Creighton, is a former Texas legislator and the author of Senate Bill 37, the law that limited shared governance . Creighton said he intended for the bill to “eliminate woke indoctrination in core courses” and give “Texans the power to report biased or inappropriate instruction.” The original text contained explicit “identity politics” restrictions that were stripped from the final version, possibly because they might not have passed legal muster. The policy he has implemented at Texas Tech, however, resembles the original version. Creighton has said he believes that it will be a “national model.” Creighton issued two memos outlining the restrictions, including one threatening faculty members that a failure to report any course content “implicated” by the policy would result in “disciplinary action.” Another announced a phaseout of all degree programs related to what the memo referred to as SOGI (“Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity”). It also formalizes a ban on “instruction that advocates for concepts of inherent racial or sexual superiority, inherent bias, or collective guilt.” In the future, the memo states, no degree “will be permitted to center on SOGI topics.” Such a ban on entire fields of study, inquiry, and discourse, Creighton said—preposterously—would foster “diversity of viewpoint.” For many years, Sara Spurgeon has taught a literature class focused on social justice and the environment. She has often assigned Ta-Nehisi Coates’s Pulitzer Prize–winning memoir Between the World and Me , but this time, the book was flagged by the bot as promoting “the belief that meritocracy is a construct of oppression designed to exploit Black bodies,” and it therefore “directly violates the system’s Prohibition of Prejudiced Advocacy.” (The word meritocracy does not appear in the book.) Creighton has insisted that “studying Black history, discussing the realities of racism, and treating every student with respect are not prohibited.” Spurgeon told me that works by science fiction and fantasy authors were also flagged. In other professors’ syllabi, the bot flagged the Pulitzer Prize–winning play Angels in America by Tony Kushner, essays by the Mexican American MacArthur genius grant recipient Sandra Cisneros, and materials related to a class about the Holocaust (that professor was told to drop material regarding Nazi persecution of LGBTQ people). Putting aside the ideological slant of the new rules, the bot, like many large language models, seems to “hallucinate,” or make mistakes. The AAUP lawsuit lists texts banned for their “sex-based ecofeminist framework” and “gendered ecofeminist frameworks.” These phrases might sound persuasively like academese, but the academics behind the lawsuit had never heard of them; these concepts “do not exist,” the complaint says. Matthew Pehl, a history professor at Tech, told me that he knew several people who’d received reports from the system that were “plainly written by an AI that had hallucinated content or confused content from one class to another.” Alan Barenberg, a history professor who specializes in the Soviet Union, was told to remove readings by the Princeton historian Joan Scott and the French philosopher Michel Foucault from his Ph.D.-level historiography class, after they were flagged by the AI—whose assessments he described to me as “completely inaccurate.” It also seemed to have mixed his course up with a different one. The texts were part of a unit of the class related to how treatment of gender in historical research has changed over time. “These things have been taught in classes for a long time,” Barenberg told me. The material is controversial, he said, only “in the eyes of a few people who aren’t even actually on campus.” “The fact that the system AI doesn’t work, that it makes inaccurate pronouncements—that’s a feature, not a bug. They don’t care if it’s accurate or not. They just want to be able to say, Look, we’re making sure that your children are not being exposed to these horrible ideas from these radical professors ,” Barenberg said. “A key part of how authoritarian systems often work is that, through the vagueness and sending up signals and vibes, they’re essentially saying, You know what not to do , but being deliberately vague about it.” Although the AI is now reviewing only some courses, the university could extend the process to more. For now, professors are the ones responsible for volunteering whether their own materials may be considered controversial. Many, unsure of what might trigger the bot, told me that they had private conversations with administrators who told them to simply self-censor and remove materials from their courses in advance, so as not to draw the wrath of leadership or lawmakers. Pehl, the history professor, told me that he did just that, and decided not to use the book Scraping By , about labor in Revolutionary-era Baltimore, because he had been planning on teaching it early in the year, which didn’t allow time for it to be reviewed first. The book differentiates between the experiences of workers based on whether they were enslaved or free, men or women. William Wenthe, a poetry professor, didn’t mark his course as potentially controversial, though he told me that he was worried: He teaches T. S. Eliot’s The Wasteland , which includes a male character from Greek mythology who becomes a woman. Could a Texan politician object to that? Censorship infantilizes students, he said: “They’re old enough to vote. They’re all old enough to fight and die for this country. And you’re treating them like babies.” Texas Tech’s censorship policy does not just affect the humanities. According to the AAUP lawsuit, medical students at the campus in El Paso are no longer permitted to learn about racial disparities in medical care or how to treat underserved populations—both major challenges in the overwhelmingly Hispanic Texas border region. At the Lubbock campus, a professor of health sciences at the medical school was told that he could not teach about transgender or intersex patients. Some professors are leaving. Breanna Harris told me she quit her job as a biology professor at the Lubbock campus in part because she says administrators informed her that she could not use the American Medical Association’s definitions of sex and gender , which, by distinguishing between the two, run afoul of Texas law. Harris’s course materials, she said, ask questions such as “How do organisms become ‘male’ or ‘female’?” and “What does that process look like biologically during development?” Lisa Limeri, a biology professor at Texas Tech who had just been awarded tenure this year, resigned for the same reason. “We are not allowed to teach topics that are relevant to things like the MCAT and being practicing medical professionals,” she told me. “We are not allowed to teach them scientifically, accurately.” A spokesperson for the university pushed back on the claim that medical students were not being taught what they would need to do their jobs: “We have tremendous confidence in our faculty and their commitment to preparing students to provide excellent care. It is important to distinguish between what our policy actually requires and restrictions that are not found anywhere in our written guidance.” According to an internal survey, more than half of Tech’s faculty are looking for work elsewhere. In a private meeting with faculty, a recording of which was shared with me, a provost acknowledged that “on average, we have 20 percent to 25 percent fewer people applying for jobs here.” When professors challenged him on why he was not fighting against censorship, the provost said he couldn’t stop it: “It’s going to happen. And so you can try to help slow or mitigate it,” he said. “Or you can bring in people who will help it happen faster. That’s the option at the moment.” Texas Tech is an R1 research university, which means that it receives a large amount of federal funding to produce significant amounts of research. But the censorship policy leaves entire fields of scientific inquiry banned, even for Ph.D. students. “America has risen to global prominence in science and scientific research because of the strength of our system,” Limeri said. “If these kinds of censorship policies were implemented everywhere, we would have a generation of students who are not learning to think critically, are not learning to think for themselves, and are not learning full and accurate scientific information.” Administrators told faculty in that private meeting not to discuss the censorship policy with students, because it might generate “a lot of fear and a lot of anger and anxiety.” T he Texas A&M system , which serves about 175,000 students, doesn’t have an AI censor. But it does have both a strict, arbitrary, and confusing censorship policy and elected leaders joining online mobs against professors. Melissa McCoul, a senior lecturer in the English department at Texas A&M’s College Station campus, has taught her course on children’s literature 11 times since arriving at the university in 2017. And she would have continued to do so, if Governor Abbott hadn’t demanded she be fired. In July 2025, Brian Harrison, a Republican state representative, reposted a slide from McCoul’s class that had been highlighted by another X user. The slide argued that queerness can be discussed in “age-appropriate” terms and that homosexuality was not an “x-rated” concept. Harrison declared that “Texans are being taxed out of their homes to fund liberal indoctrination.” McCoul immediately found herself at the mercy of a social-media mob. A little more than two weeks later, a student interrupted McCoul’s class to say that her teachings were “against the law.” After a brief exchange, McCoul asked the student to leave. In September (by which time McCoul was teaching a different class), Harrison posted a video of the summer confrontation and described the student as “OBJECTING TO TRANSGENDER INDOCTRINATION.” Harrison also posted a letter he had sent to Abbott reminding him that “during your State of the State Address, you stated that ‘any educator who tells students that boys can be girls should be fired on the spot.’” Mark Welsh, then the president of A&M, replied to Harrison’s post with a statement that the class had been canceled and that “key leaders” had been removed for allowing McCoul to teach “course content that was not consistent with the course’s published description.” Abbott joined the mob, replying, “Good. Now, fire the professor who acted contrary to Texas law.” Promptly, the university did. McCoul claims that the course never deviated from the catalog description and has sued the university for ignoring its own due-process procedures; the lawsuit is ongoing. According to her complaint, two faculty panels reviewing the incident found no good cause for her firing. Welsh has since resigned. In a motion to dismiss McCoul’s suit, filed in April, A&M states that McCoul was an untenured senior lecturer and that “Texas A&M University is entitled to state sovereign immunity as an ‘arm of the state.’” The motion also argues that “the termination was lawful and was certainly no violation of the lecturer’s academic freedom or the First Amendment.” The university alleges that McCoul “used the class as an opportunity to indoctrinate her students into transgender and LGBTQ ideology,” and that “by kicking out a student” who expressed a contrary opinion and “threatening” to kick out others, McCoul “interfered with those students’ academic freedom.” The filing also makes sure to point out that “she began the class by introducing herself as an autistic lesbian.” In December, A&M adopted a policy stating that “no system academic course will advocate race or gender ideology, or topics related to sexual orientation or gender identity.” The next month, the women’s and gender studies programs were eliminated. The policy defines gender ideology as the idea “that self-assessed gender identity should replace the biological category of sex,” whereas race ideology “attempts to shame a particular race or ethnicity, accuse them of being oppressors in a racial hierarchy or conspiracy, ascribe to them less value as contributors to society and public discourse because of their race or ethnicity, or assign them intrinsic guilt based on the actions of their presumed ancestors.” If a professor acknowledges the existence of trans people, they could be violating the first policy; if they describe race-based chattel slavery in the antebellum United States, they could be violating the second. Their livelihood might depend on how much time the governor of Texas is spending on social media that day. Leonard Bright, a tenured professor at A&M’s Bush School of Government and Public Service, is one of several other professors suing the university for its censorship policy. This year, his graduate-level course on ethics and public policy was canceled. His lawsuit says that he informed the administration that “at no point does the course require students to adopt, affirm, or reject particular beliefs regarding these topics. Students are evaluated solely on analytical rigor, use of evidence, and professional engagement.” Still, he told me, the university wouldn’t approve the class unless he provided “a detailed day-by-day description of when sexual orientation is going to come up.” And he couldn’t do that, because “this is a discussion course.” The policy raises other uncomfortable questions for Prairie View A&M, a historically Black college in the A&M system that was first established by the Reconstruction-era legislature as a segregated institution . There’s no way to even explain its existence without touching on matters that could be caricatured as “race ideology.” The difference between “advocating” and “teaching” is not clearly defined, but the way the censorship policy is being implemented makes the situation pretty clear: If you’re using material that state lawmakers agree with, that’s teaching; if you’re talking about something they object to, that’s advocacy, and you have to stop. As detailed in a complaint against Texas A&M filed by the ACLU, an English professor, Vanita Reddy, was told that the censorship policy “will not be applied to heteronormative orientation and identity,” but exclusively to “LGBTQ gender identity or sexual orientation.” George, the history professor who was told to remove several texts perceived as liberal, was allowed to teach the conservative anti-feminist activist Phyllis Schlafly’s “What’s Wrong With Equal Rights for Women?” P rofessors at UT Austin aren’t seeing their classes summarily canceled or scrubbed for forbidden terms by a censorship AI. They haven’t been told to list the dates that gender might come up. The governor hasn’t demanded the heads of any of its professors. “Gender and race ideology” have not been banned. While Texas Tech and Texas A&M received an “F” from the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, a free-speech watchdog, UT Austin earned a “D–”. What UT has done is issue a statement on “academic integrity” urging professors to “fairly present differing views and scholarly evidence on reasonably disputed matters and unsettled issues” and “to eschew topics and controversies that are not germane to the course.” No one is really sure what that means—and that may be the point. “Nobody yet has been disciplined under this policy,” Julie Minich, an English professor who focuses on Latino literature, told me. “But also, nobody wants to be the first one to be disciplined under the policy.” The university did not respond to repeated requests by phone and email to speak about this story or to a list of questions. [ Adam Serwer: Speak at your own risk ] Peter Onyisi, a physics professor, has for years used the greenhouse effect as an example of a real-world, practical effect of quantum mechanics to students. Although he does not plan to stop, he worries that administrators could argue that climate change is not “germane” to his course. But that’s not how teaching works, Onyisi pointed out: “You can’t really say, Oh, physics is in a nice little box, and it doesn’t talk to anything else .” Academic freedom is under assault in the UT system, he said, just in more “subtle” ways than elsewhere. Jim Davis, the president of UT, has justified the cuts to the core curriculum by arguing that too many courses were “ narrow .” One of Davis’s favorite examples is a class on the history of college football, although, as one professor pointed out to me, the origins of the sport offer a fascinating view into the post–Civil War economy and culture of the South, not to mention a billion-dollar industry that is a big deal at, well, UT. That’s the thing about academic inquiry: Many seemingly “narrow” questions open up much bigger ones. Davis’s example, however, may be misleading. Given that most of the courses being targeted involve the study of gender or race, “narrow” seems to refer mainly to the study of people, subjects, or works that some conservatives consider unimportant. These sweeping changes couldn’t have happened “if shared governance was still in existence,” Lauren Gutterman, the American-studies professor, told me. “S.B. 37 has changed things dramatically in just a very short period of time.” A university task force has proposed that the new core include a “Great Questions of Human Life” requirement based on texts from preapproved “great thinkers.” A preliminary list of 50 names was sent out to faculty. The list includes three Black writers (W. E. B. Du Bois, Frederick Douglass, and Toni Morrison), six women (in addition to Morrison: Mary Shelley, Simone de Beauvoir, Mary Ann Evans, Jane Austen, and Mary Wollstonecraft), and no Hispanic or Latin American authors. The only Asian author on the list is Confucius. (UT has said it “intends” to expand the list ). A “Masterworks of Literature” requirement would pull most of its readings from the same list, and divide them into the categories “American,” “British,” and “World.” The proposed “Principles of American Politics” requirement warns that the courses should “focus on issues that involve the whole country, not just one region or group.” And under its “Western Civilization” requirement, the task force observes that “Western Civilization has interacted in complex ways with other civilizations”—middle-school writing that raises the question of what counts as Western civilization , a term that the report acknowledges it cannot define. “They’re saying that they need to be broad classes that satisfy the core requirements, not narrow classes,” Minich told me. But the effect is the opposite. “Rather than having a core curriculum that reflects the diversity of the campus in the public flagship of the second-most diverse state in the country, they’re moving toward a curriculum that is much more heavily focused on the European intellectual tradition. And they are calling that ‘breadth’ and saying that courses that fall outside that intellectual tradition are ‘narrow.’” Classes that get stripped of their core designation may end up scrapped altogether, because students have limited time. Declining enrollment in non-core classes can then be an excuse to dispose of them entirely. “At the time I came here, UT was the No. 1 place to do what I do—studying Latino literature. We have this long, rich history of Latino studies,” Minich said. “I see this as a first step toward eliminating an area of study that has been historically extremely important at this university.” In July, Iván Chaar López, an expert in the history of the U.S. southern border, was denied tenure , as Inside Higher Ed reported, despite the College of Liberal Arts tenure committee voting overwhelmingly in his favor. Chaar López told me that, in a meeting with administrators that February, he was told that the president’s tenure committee “had a negative view” of his work. He is challenging the decision, and is one of several faculty members or administrators who believe that they were fired, laid off, or denied tenure because their politics were seen as left-wing or because their expertise is among the subjects the administration has turned against. “It is almost as if we are meant to teach whatever fits into a political pamphlet. But that’s not what free inquiry and free speech and academic freedom are about,” Chaar López told me. Students are getting “an education that is all about obeying.” Angela Valenzuela, a professor in the department of educational leadership and policy, said that you should not be able to “graduate from UT Austin and not know anything about anything south of the Rio Grande River and call yourself an educated person.” She added, “This is not an argument about whether or not ‘Western civilization’ should be taught. It’s an argument of whether that’s what should be exclusively taught.” UT’s quiet restructuring of the university may prove to be more effective and sustainable than the tactics at Texas Tech and Texas A&M; UT’s censorship attempts, notably, have yet to face a legal challenge. Nonetheless, professors fear that the changes will leave students without the cognitive tools or contextual information to question matters that some conservatives would prefer not be questioned. Meanwhile, resources have been directed instead toward UT Austin’s new School of Civic Leadership, which claims to promote “freedom of thought and speech.” J en Shelton , an English professor at Texas Tech, told me that her daughter had gone to college in Minnesota. “When she had her first class,” Shelton said, “she called me to say, ‘You won’t believe all the things people are allowed to say up here.’” Some conservative activists have gone beyond attacking teachers. Brian Harrison, who led the campaign against the A&M professor, railed in September against the existence of an archive of LGBTQ-history primary-source documents at the University of North Texas. The webpage describing the archive was taken down; one begins to wonder whether the state will demand the destruction of the documents themselves next. In a 2026 AAUP survey , 70 percent of Texas faculty would not recommend taking a faculty position in the state, and about 30 percent said they had experienced censorship of courses by administrators. Texas “is on the leading edge” in the field of censorship in higher education, Jonathan Friedman, who directs PEN America’s work on free expression in the United States, told me. But Texas is hardly alone. According to PEN, Alabama, Florida, Indiana, and Utah have all adopted laws that seek to limit what professors are allowed to teach and what students are allowed to study. “Notions like academic freedom and free speech on campus are all just going out the window,” Friedman said. More Republican-leaning states will likely follow. Over the past decade, some conservatives have invoked principles of academic freedom and free speech in order to subvert both. These conservatives mocked “snowflakes” and “trigger warnings,” and then passed legislation making it illegal to hurt white students’ feelings by discussing historical or contemporary events. They invoked academic freedom and then began erasing fields of study they found politically inconvenient. They railed against “indoctrination,” and then argued that the state is entitled to control everything said in the classroom. [ Kevin Carey: The logical end point of Trump’s higher-education agenda ] One might argue that progressive influence on campus had gone too far and states needed to reestablish free-speech norms eroded during the zenith of the first anti-Trump backlash. Conservative ideas do have an important place in higher education—a well-rounded education is impossible otherwise. But there is a distinction between left-wing censoriousness and actual state censorship. Todd Wolfson, the president of AAUP, told me that he would be “the first to admit” that he witnessed people and ideas being “shut down from discussion” on campus. But, he said, “there’s no comparison in the ability and attempt to dictate ideas. Just none. One was informal, and the other is now formal and legal.” He continued, “I think it’s a fantasy to say that what happened then has any relationship to the extremism that we’re seeing right now.” The right-wing assault on higher education may be rooted in college-educated voters’ shift to the left. If one blames that shift on left-wing professors, then purging them from academia could change the way educated people vote. But educational polarization is a global phenomenon, and evidence shows that college does not alter students’ political beliefs as much as people assume. Attacking universities is more likely to simply degrade the quality of education than it is to help Republicans at the polls. Besides, in Texas, many students arrive as conservatives and stay that way. Many students have protested the new censorship policies, while others have enforced them, as demonstrated by the undergraduates turning their professors in for violations. University leaders have occasionally attempted to disguise their campaigns as an effort to better prepare Texas students for the workforce. Texas Tech Chancellor Brandon Creighton said that there was “quite a bit of garbage in curriculum all over university campuses all across America,” and that Tech would “remain the tip of the spear on producing the highest degree of value.” But the value of even the hardest STEM degree will be degraded if courses in those fields are censored for being politically inconvenient. And regardless, the quality of an education is not determined by the wealth you subsequently accumulate. So what can be done? Legal precedent seems to be on the side of people challenging the censorship policies, at least at Tech and A&M. The Supreme Court has held that academic freedom is a “special concern” that is “of transcendent value to all of us.” Florida, during litigation over the Stop WOKE Act, a similar ban on “divisive concepts,” tried to argue that the First Amendment didn’t apply to professors at state schools, because they were government employees. The Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals rejected that argument , concluding that “if the history of that Amendment tells us anything, it is that the government cannot forbid what it perceives as heresy.” The current right-wing majority on the Supreme Court, however, has shown itself willing to ignore the plain text of the Constitution where the latest culture-war fixation is concerned. “You have to go back to the loyalty oath cases of the Cold War period to see relatively analogous situations where the government was trying to silence academics with viewpoints that they didn’t like,” Emerson Sykes, an attorney with the ACLU, told me. “But even in those cases, we did not see the sort of brazen attempt to ban particular ideas or ideologies and scrub them from the public record or from public education.” Sykes cautioned me that although academic freedom interacts with the First Amendment, they are not synonymous. The Eleventh Circuit ruling found that state governments can “make ordinary curriculum decisions (like which majors or courses to offer), or otherwise ensure competent academic instruction.” For that reason, UT Austin’s structural changes are likely more resistant to legal challenge. Those who wish to oppose them may have to find other means, such as labor organizing or politics. That will be a monumental task—especially as universities are relying more and more on tenuously employed adjunct professors. In the meantime, the Trump administration has been meddling in higher education at the federal level—using grants to pressure universities into changing whom they admit and what they teach and research, and going after foreign students for their politics. The degradation of free speech doesn’t stop in Texas. And it won’t stay on campus either. This article originally misstated the date when the professor Sara Spurgeon first had to submit her course materials through a portal for review.

items.title: Comment lutter contre la tuberculose de l’olivier signalée à Mahdia et Sfax
items.description: Le Dr Noureddine Nasr, consultant international en développement agricole, a affirmé que la tuberculose de l’olivier, qui a fait l’objet récemment d’alertes phytosanitaires importantes dans les gouvernorats de Mahdia et de Sfax, n’est pas une maladie nouvelle, contrairement à ce qui est affirmé par certains sur les réseaux sociaux, précisant qu’il s’agit d’une maladie bactérienne connue de longue date dans le bassin méditerranéen. Cette maladie causée par la bactérie Pseudomonas savastanoi n’a aucun lien, non plus, avec la cochenille du cactus, qui a ravagé des milliers d’hectares de figues de Barbarie ces dernières années en Tunisie, a-t-il ajouté, lors de son intervention sur la radio Diwan FM, ce dimanche 11 octobre 2026. La bactérie responsable de la maladie est associée aux oliviers et est présente dans plusieurs pays méditerranéens, notamment la Tunisie, la Grèce, l’Italie et la France, a-t-il encore précisé, soulignant que l’infection peut affecter la productivité des arbres. L’expert international a appelé les agriculteurs à respecter un ensemble de mesures préventives pour protéger les oliveraies et limiter la propagation de l’infection entre les arbres, soulignant l’importance d’une intervention précoce et de l’adoption de pratiques agricoles saines. Dans ce contexte, il a insisté sur la nécessité d’éviter l’achat et la plantation de vieux oliviers déracinés — connus localement sous le nom de «Zitoun El Koub» — signalant que le transfert d’arbres infectés peut contribuer à la propagation de la bactérie vers d’autres arbres dans d’autres. Dr Nasr a également recommandé de s’approvisionner en plants exclusivement auprès de pépinières agréées et contrôlées par le ministère de l’Agriculture, tout en vérifiant les documents officiels et en évitant de traiter avec des pépinières informelles ou non autorisées. Il a, ensuite, mis en garde contre les risques de transmission de la bactérie par le biais des outils de taille, préconisant d’attribuer des outils spécifiques à chaque ouvrier et de les désinfecter conformément aux recommandations techniques en vigueur. Il a également conseillé de commencer par tailler les arbres sains avant de passer à ceux suspectés d’être infectés ou déjà atteints, tout en recommandant de retirer les branches et les chancres infectés et de les traiter selon les directives phytosanitaires officielles, en les brûlant immédiatement sur place, au pied de l’arbre, tout en évitant de les transporter sans précaution d’un champ à l’autre, afin de limiter les risques de propagation de l'infection. Il convient, par ailleurs, de prêter attention au rôle de certains insectes dans la transmission de la bactérie, sachant que la rapidité de propagation de la maladie exige vigilance, suivi périodique de l’état des arbres et intervention dès l’apparition des symptômes. Ces recommandations s’inscrivent dans le cadre d’un appel à renforcer la prévention et à protéger la récolte d’olives en Tunisie, en sensibilisant les agriculteurs aux modes de transmission de la maladie et en adoptant des méthodes de lutte fondées sur des directives techniques spécialisées. I. B. L’article Comment lutter contre la tuberculose de l’olivier signalée à Mahdia et Sfax est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Intercity transport suspended in Lahore, bus terminals reportedly sealed
items.description: LAHORE: Intercity bus services from Lahore to several destinations across the country were suspended on Sunday after the administration reportedly sealed all general bus terminals in the city late on Saturday night, leaving passengers stranded and disrupting travel. The closures affected passengers travelling to Islamabad, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Sindh, southern Punjab and other parts of central Punjab. Several passengers reported difficulties after their tickets were cancelled and transport services suspended. Meanwhile, major private bus operators, including Faisal Movers and Daewoo, suspended their services amid reports of restrictions on public transport movement on motorways and national highways. Representatives of Faisal Movers and Daewoo told Dawn that their services had been suspended and buses were not being dispatched due to the restrictions. However, motorway police spokesperson Imran Shah told Dawn that motorways and highways were open to traffic and that he was unaware of any directions to suspend bus services. Another motorway police official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said buses were not operating on motorways or highways because of the PTI’s protest call. He added that people travelling in private vehicles could use the roads. Punjab Transport Department Secretary Imran Sikandar Baloch was unavailable for comment despite repeated attempts to contact him on his mobile phone. The development comes as the PTI launched its march on October 4 despite warnings from the Centre. So far, the march — being carried out to demand Imran’s release — has remained within KP, where the PTI is in power. A day earlier, containers were transported to Swabi Interchange — where the PTI had called on its workers to gather — as well as the Indus River bridge on the M-1 Motorway to block the party’s march, but the motorway and the Grand Trunk Road remain open to traffic.

items.title: Drame conjugal a Sénégal : Cheikhou Oumar Ndiaye poignardé à mort dans son sommeil par sa seconde épouse
items.description: Dans la nuit du jeudi 8 au vendredi 9 octobre 2026, le paisible village de Sam Ndiaye, situé dans la commune de Fandène, a été le théâtre d'un homicide conjugal d'une rare violence. Cheikhou Oumar Ndiaye, un chauffeur et cultivateur d'une quarantaine d'années, a été poignardé à mort dans son sommeil par sa seconde épouse, Asta Dia, sur fond de différend familial. Mortellement touché de deux coups de couteau, ce père de six enfants s'est effondré après avoir désigné son agressrice dans un dernier souffle, laissant une communauté sous le choc et une suspecte désormais aux mains de la gendarmerie. Rien ne laissait présager l'issue fatale de cette soirée dans le village de Sam Ndiaye, situé sur l'axe Ndiobène. En début de soirée, Cheikhou Oumar Ndiaye, conducteur de bus de la ligne 10 du réseau urbain de Thiès et cultivateur, regagnait le domicile conjugal après avoir travaillé dans les champs familiaux en compagnie de ses deux épouses. Cependant, une vive altercation a rapidement éclaté au sein du foyer. Asta Dia, sa seconde épouse âgée d'une trentaine d'années et originaire de Mballène, l'accusait d'avoir battu son fils né d'un précédent mariage, une imputation que le chef de famille réfutait catégoriquement. La tension s'est accrue lorsque la présence d'une arme blanche dissimulée par Asta Dia sous son pagne ou sous un oreiller a été repérée. Informée de la menace, la mère du défunt a alerté le frère aîné de Cheikhou Oumar Ndiaye, qui s'est rendu sur place pour sermonner le couple et confisquer le couteau. Pensant la situation apaisée après cette intervention familiale, Cheikhou Oumar Ndiaye s'est endormi sur le dos dans sa chambre. Cependant, la mise en cause, enceinte de son premier enfant avec la victime, est revenue à la charge au cœur de la nuit. Après avoir confié son fils à des voisins, elle s'est procuré un second couteau avant de revenir sur les lieux. Surprenant son époux endormi, elle lui a asséné froidement deux coups de couteau, dont l'un s'est avéré mortel. Grièvement blessé et perdant abondamment son sang, Cheikhou Oumar Ndiaye a réussi à se traîner jusqu'à l'entrée de la concession en criant « Asta raynama » (« Asta m'a tué ») avant de s'écrouler. À la suite de son acte, la suspecte s'est enfuie avec son fils pour se réfugier dans une maison voisine, où elle a été rapidement interpellée par les gendarmes de Fandène. Placée en garde à vue sous la qualification de meurtre aggravé (uxoricide), elle fait l'objet d'une enquête judiciaire sous la direction du parquet compétent. Inhumé le lendemain, le défunt laisse derrière lui six orphelins. Témoignant du passé tumultueux du couple, la sœur du défunt, K. Ndiaye, a rappelé qu'Asta Dia avait déjà brandi une arme blanche lors d'une dispute précédente, avant d'exprimer la douleur de toute une communauté : « Elle n'a pas tué Cheikhou, mais toute une famille ». L’article Drame conjugal a Sénégal : Cheikhou Oumar Ndiaye poignardé à mort dans son sommeil par sa seconde épouse est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Labé : un adolescent de 14 ans grièvement brûlé à Kouroula, un jeune de 18 ans interpellé
items.description: Un apprenti réparateur d’appareils électroniques âgé de 14 ans a été grièvement brûlé vendredi 9 octobre 2026, au quartier Kouroula, dans la commune urbaine de Labé. Selon le maître de la victime, un jeune de 18 ans l’aurait volontairement incendié alors qu’il tentait d’enlever de la peinture sur son corps avec de l’essence. Le suspect a été interpellé par les gendarmes et serait en cours d’audition. Les faits se sont produits dans un atelier de réparation d’appareils électroniques où travaillait Mamadou Saidou Diallo, la jeune victime. L’adolescent aurait été atteint à plusieurs parties du corps, notamment à la tête, à la gorge, à la poitrine et aux bras. Joint au sujet de l’incident, Mamadou Saliou Diallo, maître de l’apprenti, explique que l’adolescent avait reçu de la peinture sur le corps au cours d’une opération de remise en état d’un téléviseur. « On dépannait un poste téléviseur et, au finish, il fallait le revêtir de peinture. C’est dans cette opération que le petit a eu cette peinture sur le corps », a-t-il raconté. Selon son témoignage, la victime cherchait ensuite à enlever la peinture à l’aide d’essence lorsqu’un jeune de 18 ans, identifié sous le prénom de Kaba, aurait acheté des allumettes avant de mettre le feu sur lui. Le maître de la victime affirme qu’aucune altercation n’avait précédé les faits. « Il n’y a pas eu de discussion entre eux, ni rien. Le présumé auteur n’est même pas dans mon atelier. Il était venu jouer au casino et il loge non loin de l’hôpital régional de Labé », a-t-il précisé. La victime prise en charge à l’hôpital régional Après l’incident, Mamadou Saidou Diallo a été évacué au service de traumatologie de l’hôpital régional de Labé pour recevoir des soins. D’après son maître, les médecins se sont montrés rassurants quant à sa prise en charge. Lors d’un échange avec l’adolescent le lendemain des faits, celui-ci était conscient. « Les médecins l’ont traité et ils m’ont dit être en mesure de le soigner convenablement. Ce matin, j’ai échangé avec lui et il est conscient », a indiqué Mamadou Saliou Diallo. Le suspect interpellé par les gendarmes Concernant le jeune mis en cause, le maître de la victime affirme que celui-ci aurait envisagé de rentrer chez lui après l’hospitalisation de l’adolescent. Il aurait finalement été interpellé par les gendarmes. « C’est entre-temps que les gendarmes l’ont interpellé. Il est actuellement en audition afin de déterminer ce qui l’a poussé à commettre cet acte », a-t-il ajouté. Pour l’heure, les circonstances précises de cet incident ainsi que les motivations du geste présumé restent à établir par les services compétents. Le jeune de 18 ans est présumé innocent jusqu’à l’établissement éventuel de sa culpabilité par la justice. Alpha Moussa Dieng, correspondant régional à Labé L’article Labé : un adolescent de 14 ans grièvement brûlé à Kouroula, un jeune de 18 ans interpellé est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .
